docs.title: What Is Sensoraia?
docs.text:
Sensoraia is an AI-enabled, in-flight sensing suite for connecting cameras, microphones and supported processing to an aircraft's onboard computer. It takes care of requesting captures, saving the results and keeping the available flight information with them. It also connects live sensor processing back to the flight: MORA can exchange data with the airborne aircraft while the mission is running, not just collect files for you to inspect after landing. The result is more useful than a folder of photographs whose story you have to reconstruct afterwards.

You might use it to look for vehicles with a neural network, listen for an alarm, inspect thermal observations, or feed supported live results into the next flight-plan decision. You choose the sensors and the job; Sensoraia provides a shared way to connect them to the flight.

New to the names? The Sensoraia glossary explains the shared vocabulary and each module's terms.

docs.title: I Just want the code
docs.text: So in a hurry huh? Just want the code, find all sourcecode on github. But advised is to read the getting started page before you confuse yourself.

docs.title: Spend Less Time Joining The Pieces
docs.text: A sensor, an AI model, an autopilot and an onboard computer do not automatically agree on when to observe, how to process the result or which flight position belongs to it. Sensoraia handles the shared coordination, so supported modules can concentrate on their sensing and processing jobs.

docs.title: Keep The Context, Not Just The Picture
docs.text: A photograph becomes much more useful when you can relate it to the aircraft's position, attitude and capture request. Sensoraia records the available context in image metadata and reports what completed. When timing or calibration is uncertain, it keeps that distinction visible rather than turning an estimate into a promise.

docs.title: Explore Before You Connect Hardware
docs.text: Run the suite on a Linux PC with a simulated aircraft and camera views made from cached aerial imagery. Follow a request through capture, processing and supported mission results, then move to your real onboard computer and sensors. Your first experiment does not need a flying aircraft. The propeller is welcome to sit this one out.

docs.title: The Same Application Code, Simulated Or Airborne
docs.text:
Local simulation runs the same production application source code as the software built for MORA, not a separate demonstration reimplementation. The simulated aircraft and camera inputs stand in for physical hardware; the capture coordination, processing and result-handling code remain the application you are preparing to deploy.

The PC and ARM64 executables are different builds, and real sensors have their own drivers, timing and calibration. Simulation lets you exercise the application workflow before making those hardware connections.

docs.title: Let Your PC Do The Heavy Lifting
docs.text: Use the cores on your PC to build in parallel, including cross-compiling the ARM64 applications for MORA. You do not need to wait for the small companion board to compile its own software or install a development toolchain there: build on the fast machine, deploy the ready-to-run binaries, and keep MORA focused on sensing and processing. The build instructions use make -j"$(nproc)" to use your PC's available CPU cores.

docs.title: A Live Conversation With The Aircraft
docs.text:
During flight, the controller sends pose information and capture requests to MORA. USHER coordinates the sensor work and returns supported completion or target-point results. A compatible flight plan can use fresh results to update a waypoint, follow a returned point or choose its next mission action. The flight controller remains responsible for flying the aircraft.

This is live, real-time interaction while flying: sensing, supported processing and mission decisions can happen during the flight, without waiting for a post-flight download. Actual update rates depend on the sensor, model and available computing resources; live operation is not a guarantee of hard real-time deadlines.

docs.title: Neural Networks Can Take Part In The Flight
docs.text:
Neural-network processing is not limited to an offline report. Spottercam produces vehicle detections from the IMX500 during capture. Its built-in output is image detections and metadata; geographic target publishing for flight response is an additional integration step. Diplacam's experimental neural planner can return XY points that the supplied rotorcraft flight plan follows and refreshes in simulation. With the appropriate result interface and flight-plan logic, observations can therefore influence mission behavior while the aircraft is airborne.

You decide which results the flight plan may act on. A detection alone does not command a maneuver, and a network does not take over the motors. Each module's guide explains what it currently returns and its qualification limits; Diplacam is experimental, and LOOM's guarded return-vector integration awaits its trained homing model and physical accuracy validation.

docs.title: How The Hardware Fits Together
docs.text:
Think of it as three parts with different jobs:

  1. The flight controller flies the aircraft. Your flight plan or operator requests a capture at the appropriate moment.
  2. MORA carries the sensor software. MORA is the aircraft's companion- computer role, not a particular board. Sensoraia uses the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W as its initial, resource-constrained reference platform; another suitable compute board can fill the role. It connects to the flight controller over UART and to cameras or microphones through their own interfaces.
  3. USHER coordinates the work. USHER is Sensoraia's service on MORA: it receives the request, works with the selected sensor, saves the result with its context, and sends completion or supported target results back to the flight controller. The connection works in both directions.

Sensoraia is the whole suite, MORA is the computer, and USHER is the coordinating service. Three names, not three things you must learn before you can take a picture.

The current ready-made ARM64 build, package and setup instructions target 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS Trixie on the Pi Zero 2 W. That is a starting point, not a hardware lock-in: other Linux compute boards can run Sensoraia when their architecture, OS libraries, sensor drivers, interfaces and available resources are supported or adapted. They need a matching build and deployment configuration; Pi-specific instructions do not automatically apply.

Paparazzi examples connect this workflow to simulated and real flight controllers. You can also run individual sensor tools from a terminal. You do not need every sensor or every module to make a useful setup.

docs.title: What Could You Do With It?
docs.text:
Search for vehicles with live AI. Spottercam runs a compatible trained vehicle network on the IMX500, keeping its detections tied to captured images. Use the results for live review and recording; add a qualified geographic-target integration when your mission should act on a location.

Respond to supported observations in flight. Feed fresh target or planner results into compatible flight-plan logic: update a waypoint, follow up an observation or choose a mission branch. Each backend defines what it returns; the flight controller retains navigation and control.

Listen while you fly. EARcam detects an alarm tone and combines useful sound readings from different positions into an acoustic search estimate.

Explore thermal targets. Save thermal images, examine supported temperature samples and regions, and use measured lens/mounting calibration when projecting thermal observations onto the ground. A warm patch is a candidate, not an automatic identification of a particular object.

Add the sensor your mission needs. The architecture separates sensor adapters, processing and the flight-controller protocol. That gives developers a place to integrate a gas, particle or radiation sensor and define the result a mission may use. These are extension examples, not built-in Geiger, gas or particle drivers; new sensors need an adapter and an agreed data/result contract. It is extensible, not a universal plug-and-play driver collection.

Try a new idea without changing the flight interface. Use the local simulation with the same production application source, then connect MORA and the actual sensor. Check both your result handling and the physical sensor's behavior before relying on the combination.

Build better datasets and keep useful evidence. Original photographs, metadata and permitted MIMIC imagery can support external model training and evaluation. PANGEA maps and tiles can help with scene selection and annotation context; they are an additional tool, not the main mission. Training still needs suitable labels, imagery rights and independent evaluation, and camera-view models need representative camera-view inputs.

Keep conventional capture alongside AI. Use supported visible-light and thermal cameras for ordinary photographs too. You choose where inference adds value instead of making every capture depend on a model.

These are options, not a checklist. A dependable setup with one sensor is a perfectly good place to begin.

docs.title: Start Small, Grow Deliberately
docs.text:
If you are curious, explore the example below. If you already have a sensor in mind, choose its guide next. When you are ready to try it yourself, the installation guide walks you through a PC build, a local simulation and deployment to MORA.

Sensoraia helps you collect and interpret observations; it is not a flight controller or certified navigation, rescue or measurement system. Real-world accuracy depends on your sensors, calibration and timing. The guides explain those limits where they matter, so you can make informed choices as you go.

docs.title: Try Sensoraia With Paparazzi
docs.text:
Fly a complete mission from takeoff to landing in Paparazzi NPS—even without a MORA board or physical camera attached. Paparazzi flies the simulated aircraft; USHER supplies sensor observations and target updates over a simulated local UART (/tmp/usher-sim) or a real FTDI cable to MORA.

Prepare your first demo | Glossary | Install Sensoraia

docs.title: Quick Start: Install Links With ./kickstart.sh
docs.text:
With Paparazzi already installed at ~/paparazzi, build the native PC applications and link the Sensoraia configurations into Paparazzi:

make native
./kickstart.sh

./kickstart.sh installs userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_conf.xml and the unified userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_control_panel.xml into ~/paparazzi/conf/, links the self-contained SENSORAIA flight plans, airframes, radios, and telemetry profiles, and selects the demo configuration (preserving any previous conf.xml and control_panel.xml links). Prefer creating the symlinks yourself or keeping your active conf.xml untouched? Use ./kickstart.sh --no-activate or follow the exact manual ln -s commands in Manual Symlink Setup.

docs.title: Start A Simulated Flight (Takeoff To Landing)
docs.text:
1. Launch Paparazzi Center: cd ~/paparazzi && ./paparazzi.
  2. In Config, ensure userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_conf.xml and userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_control_panel.xml are selected.
  3. Pick the aircraft for the camera you want to fly (for example Easystar_3_SPOTTERCAM or Bebop_DIPLACAM), select target nps, and click Build.
  4. Open the Session tab, select the matching Sensoraia \<Camera> NPS session, and click Execute.
  5. In PprzGCS, wait for live aircraft telemetry and a valid 3D GPS fix (Holding point or Ground standby), then click Takeoff.
  6. Watch the aircraft climb, fly its camera mission, and complete its landing sequence (Land $\rightarrow$ Final $\rightarrow$ Flare on fixed-wing demos, or Return $\rightarrow$ Land Here on Bebop_DIPLACAM), then click Stop in Center before starting another session.

Starting the session programs does not command takeoff. Do not start a second USHER or simulator on the same endpoints. For MORA hardware-in-the-loop over an FTDI cable, select Sensoraia MORA desk NPS (which omits PC USHER so nps connects straight to /dev/ttyUSB0). See the complete flight walkthrough.

docs.title: Choose Your Camera Demo
docs.text:
Camera / Mode Supplied Aircraft Paparazzi Center Session What Happens In Flight Spottercam Easystar_3_SPOTTERCAM (Fixed wing) Sensoraia Spottercam NPS Captures mock vehicle views, runs native YOLO11n ONNX detection, and projects ranked hits onto T1..T5 AI Camera Easystar_3_AICAM (Fixed wing) Sensoraia AIcam NPS Periodic wings-level visible-camera survey photos tagged with EXIF flight pose LWIRcam Easystar_3_LWIRCAM (Fixed wing) Sensoraia LWIRcam NPS Thermal survey capture and session protocol flow CHDKbridge Easystar_3_CHDKCAM (Fixed wing) Sensoraia CHDKcam NPS Ticketed optical zoom, distance-triggered survey photos, and pre-landing lens retraction EARcam Easystar_3_EARCAM (Fixed wing) Sensoraia EARcam NPS Flower search over a simulated acoustic beacon and guarded TARGET waypoint update LOOMcam Easystar_3_LOOMCAM (Fixed wing) Sensoraia LOOMcam NPS Outbound reference archiving (START) followed by return-leg evaluation (STOP) MIMIC / PANGEA Easystar_3_MIMIC (Fixed wing) Sensoraia MIMIC PANGEA NPS Renders camera views from cached aerial tiles and reconstructs a georeferenced photo map Diplacam Bebop_DIPLACAM (Rotorcraft) Sensoraia Diplacam NPS Native GP/diffusion planner refreshing eight 2 m sampling waypoints (P1..P8)

Fixed-wing flight plans and the Bebop_DIPLACAM rotorcraft flight plan are not interchangeable: always pair a flight plan with the matching vehicle firmware.

docs.title: Add The Paparazzi Module To Your Own Aircraft
docs.text:
The supplied Easystar_* and Bebop_DIPLACAM demo aircraft already include everything needed. When adding Sensoraia to your own Paparazzi aircraft:

  1. Point Paparazzi at Sensoraia's shared protocol headers/sources: Export SENSORAIA_SRC=/path/to/sensoraia in the environment before building your aircraft in Paparazzi Center or make. digital_cam_uart compiles usher_protocol.c and camera_control.c directly from $SENSORAIA_SRC/src while preserving Paparazzi's standard dc.c/dc.h boundary.
  2. Add digital_cam_uart to your airframe XML (<target name="ap"> and <target name="nps">):
<module name="digital_cam_uart">
  <!-- Hardware autopilot target ("ap"): select the FC UART wired to MORA's 3.3 V GPIO14/15 -->
  <configure name="CAMERA_PORT" value="uart4"/>
  <!-- Stream periodic pose updates (required by EARcam and pose-aligned sensors) -->
  <define name="DIGITAL_CAM_UART_POSE_STREAM" value="1"/>
  <!-- Optional default camera bitmask (1=CHDK, 2=AIcam/Spotter/LOOM, 4=LWIR, 8=EARcam, 16=Diplacam) -->
  <define name="DIGITAL_CAM_UART_CAMERA_MASK" value="2"/>
</module>

Do not enable a second conflicting digital_cam_* transport in the same target. On the nps simulation target, CAMERA_PORT is replaced automatically by the local /tmp/usher-sim bridge (or your FTDI cable). 3. Add digital_cam_point in your flight plan XML whenever your mission consumes geographic target points returned by USHER (EARcam, Spottercam, LWIRcam, LOOMcam, or Diplacam):

<modules>
  <module name="digital_cam_point"/>
</modules>

Use uart_cam_ctrl_set_camera_mask(...) to choose which camera triggers, digital_cam_uart_start(CAM) / digital_cam_uart_stop(CAM) for session sensors, and cam_point_fresh(CAM) + cam_point_valid(CAM) + cam_point_to_waypoint(CAM, WP_TARGET) + cam_point_consume(CAM) to validate and apply returned target coordinates safely without altering flight altitude.

docs.title: MIMIC And PANGEA
docs.text:
Cache aerial imagery over the example route and surrounding camera footprint in pprzgcs before starting. The session renders camera-view photographs from the aircraft pose, and PANGEA works from those saved photographs, not by stitching the provider's original tiles directly.

Use the MIMIC guide for cache preparation and PANGEA for map inputs and output files. Missing terrain imagery is a capture problem to resolve, not a reason to substitute invented field texture.

docs.title: Understand Waypoint Updates
docs.text:
An observation, an accepted point and a navigation decision are different events. A GCS shot marker records an admitted trigger, not necessarily a saved photograph. Moving a target waypoint does not itself select a block or tell the aircraft to visit it.

The UART module can suppress shot reports independently of triggering and returned results. The Diplacam demo uses this to avoid dense yellow shot markers; see reporting controls for airframe defaults, flight-plan calls and the live GCS setting.

The flight plan retains control of the route and flight altitude. Invalid, stale or unconfirmed points must not be treated as new targets. A normal mission can finish without a usable detection or sound fix.

docs.title: MORA In The Loop
docs.text: Use the Laptop to MORA desk test to connect NPS through an FTDI cable to real USHER. It includes the setup illustration, 5 V power and 3.3 V UART pin table, dedicated Center session and mock-then-real capture steps. This is a supported user workflow, not a private regression procedure.

docs.title: If The Demo Does Not Start
docs.text: Check that the configuration selects the intended flight plan, every session program remains running, and no earlier session owns the ports. Read the first reported error rather than starting duplicate programs. Module guides explain their specific model, cache and sensor requirements.

docs.title: Control A Canon Camera From A Flight Plan
docs.text:
The supported CHDK path can request optical zoom and powered lens retraction through USHER. These are separate from taking a photograph. The flight controller sends a request; CHDKbridge performs the camera operation on MORA and reports its outcome.

Canon setup | Camera-control terms

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Use a supported Canon camera with the correct stable CHDK build already running, matching FC/USHER software and the live CHDK backend. Check one standalone camera operation on the bench before adding it to a mission.

Other camera backends currently report these controls as unsupported. Mock camera sessions do not demonstrate mechanical zoom or retraction.

docs.title: Use The Supplied Example
docs.text:
The example is examples/paparazzi/conf/flight_plans/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_uart_cam_ctrl_demo.xml. Install the Paparazzi examples, then inspect its ticketed camera-control blocks with your aircraft configuration. It is an integration example, not a complete takeoff-and-landing mission.

Camera actions must not remove the aircraft's normal navigation guidance or make stable flight depend on a camera responding.

docs.title: Choose An Action
docs.text:
Action Meaning Important Distinction Zoom 0 Minimum optical zoom Not lens retraction Zoom 128 Middle of the normalized control range Not a guaranteed magnification ratio Zoom 255 Maximum optical zoom Actual steps depend on the camera Retract Request playback mode while keeping power on Confirmation is mode evidence, not a lens-position measurement

A later capture can extend the lens again. Mechanical retraction delay also depends on the camera's menu setting; see powered lens retraction.

docs.title: Request Once, Then Read The Result
docs.text:
For flight-plan authors, the existing digital_cam_uart interface provides:

camera_request = uart_cam_ctrl_zoom(USHER_CAMERA_MASK_CHDK, 128);
camera_request = uart_cam_ctrl_retract(USHER_CAMERA_MASK_CHDK);

These are alternative examples, not a sequence to send together. Keep the returned uint32_t ticket. A zero ticket means the request was not sent; a nonzero ticket means admitted, not completed.

In XML, use a one-shot statement for the chosen action:

<call_once
  fun="camera_request = uart_cam_ctrl_retract(USHER_CAMERA_MASK_CHDK)"/>

Declare camera_request in the plan's variables and include the control header as shown in the supplied example. Do not resend an action on every control tick.

Read uart_cam_ctrl_command_pending(camera_request) while waiting, then inspect uart_cam_ctrl_command_result(camera_request). A finished wait is not success. If a later action depends on the camera, provide an explicit failure branch while preserving appropriate aircraft guidance.

docs.title: Understand The Outcome
docs.text:
Outcome Meaning NOT_SENT No admitted command; inspect configuration/readiness PENDING Still waiting for an outcome APPLIED The backend confirmed the defined effect BUSY The camera could not accept this operation UNSUPPORTED This backend does not implement it INVALID_VALUE The requested value was not accepted FAILED Execution reported failure UNKNOWN Completion could not be established; do not assume nothing happened

A timeout does not prove the camera never acted. Avoid automatic replay of an ambiguous physical operation. Check the camera and diagnostics before deciding what the mission should do next.

docs.title: Check Before Onboard Use
docs.text: Confirm actual camera behaviour, power, USB reliability and the intended failure response with your setup. A GCS message or successful compilation does not measure lens position, mechanical timing or flight readiness.

docs.title: Try Different Lenses And Shutters
docs.text:
The lens emulator adds declared optical and exposure effects to supported MIMIC photographs. Use it to compare views, not to claim a physically calibrated camera. The original clean photo remains available.

MIMIC flight setup | Lens terms | LOOM flight camera selection

docs.title: Run With USHER
docs.text:
Build on the PC, then start a local camera peer with a supplied profile:

make -j32 usher soda camera-lens
./usher --local --mock-map --debug --mock-lens ./bin/camera_lens_aicam.json

Connect your NPS aircraft using the MIMIC walkthrough, but do not also start a second session-managed USHER. Start with a single AIcam photo at a suitable simulated pose.

To try the wider fisheye profile, restart the peer using bin/camera_lens_fisheye160.json. Its quoted 160 degrees is diagonal, not horizontal. A wider view needs more cached surrounding imagery.

docs.title: Compare The Two Images
docs.text:
For a clean capture such as ma000006.jpg, the processed companion is ma000006.lens.jpg. Open both at the same scale. USHER selects the derivative before AIcam/LOOM saved-image consumers: outbound LOOM reference links, return-phase neural inference, and SODA all see the same processed photo, only after successful emulation. Real hardware captures are unaffected.

Image Keep It For Original .jpg The clean camera view and available flight metadata .lens.jpg The declared optical/exposure experiment

Check the current log and file time if processing fails. An old derivative left on disk is not a new successful result. Different profiles use the same derivative name, so save comparison copies before processing again.

docs.title: Process A Saved MIMIC Photo
docs.text:
./bin/soda --local --aicam \
  --lens-profile ./bin/camera_lens_aicam.json \
  --lens-cache "$HOME/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map" /absolute/path/ma000006.jpg

Use an original MIMIC photo with its metadata intact and the same suitable terrain cache. This does not take a new photo or change the aircraft's altitude.

docs.title: Choose Effects Deliberately
docs.text:
Make a copy of a supplied JSON profile before changing it. Compare one effect at a time so you know what caused the difference.

For example, copy bin/camera_lens_aicam.json to your own my-lens.json. Keep the other fields in this complete profile and change selected values; do not replace it with an incomplete JSON fragment.

Effect What To Look For Exposure/brightness Lost shadow or highlight detail Exposure duration and speed Motion blur across the ground Distortion or fisheye field of view Bent lines and changed ground coverage Chromatic aberration Colour separation near edges Vibration Wobble and blur Rolling shutter Different row times causing geometric skew

docs.title: Which Settings Change The Picture?
docs.text:
Profile Key Meaning exposure_ev Brightness offset; 0 is the baseline exposure_s Exposure duration in seconds, not milliseconds motion_scale Scale of the aircraft-translation motion effect shutter global or rolling readout_s Time across rolling readout, separate from exposure duration vibration_deg, vibration_hz Angular vibration size and frequency samples Maximum temporal samples; actual count follows predicted image motion vignetting, optical_blur_px Residual corner shading and lens softness sensor_full_well_e, sensor_read_noise_e Effective shot/read noise after camera processing isp_sharpen Luma sharpening strength

Keep brightness fixed and compare exposure_s values such as 0.002 and 0.02 with motion enabled. The result also depends on recorded speed and AGL: a stationary view need not blur like a fast low pass. Restart the local peer with --mock-lens /absolute/path/my-lens.json, or use that file with the saved-photo command's --lens-profile.

The height used comes from the photograph's AGL information. Selecting an example profile does not make the simulated aircraft fly at that profile's example height. A transformed image cannot recover terrain outside the available source imagery.

docs.title: Pi Zero 2 W Resource Baseline
docs.text: The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is the 512 MB reference used when considering onboard resource limits; it is not the only board that can run Sensoraia. Begin these experiments on the PC. Large images, wide fisheye views and multiple temporal samples can be expensive. Check actual combined camera, analysis and operating-system use on the intended MORA board; a successful PC example is not an onboard throughput measurement.

docs.title: Profile Reference
docs.text:
Profiles are JSON objects with "schema": "USHER_LENS_PROFILE_V1". Unknown keys, nonfinite numbers, wrong types, and out-of-range values are errors. Omitted optional keys use the defaults below. Copy a supplied profile and edit it; validate before flying:

./bin/camera_lens --validate-profile /absolute/path/flight-camera.json
Key Units, accepted values, and default name, calibration Nonempty text, at most 160 characters; record the camera/mode and measurement provenance model brown (default) or fisheye horizontal_fov_deg, vertical_fov_deg Brown full field of view, 1..170 degrees; defaults 66.3, 52.3 diagonal_fov_deg Fisheye full diagonal field of view, 1..170 degrees; default 160 distortion Brown [k1,k2,p1,p2,k3] (five zeros by default), or fisheye [k1,k2,k3,k4]; each -2..2 output_width, output_height Both null/omitted (keep input dimensions), or both integers 2..4096; product at most 8,388,608 pixels chromatic_aberration Relative red/blue ray scaling, 0..0.01; default 0.0005 exposure_s Seconds, 0.000001..1; default 0.002 exposure_ev Relative exposure stops, -8..8; default 0 shutter rolling (default) or global readout_s Seconds across rolling readout, 0..0.2; default 0.02; must be positive for rolling shutter, ignored for global readout_direction top_to_bottom (default) or bottom_to_top motion_scale Ground-velocity multiplier, 0..10; default 1 angular_rate_deg_s Constant roll, pitch, yaw Euler rates, each -360..360 degrees/s; default [0,0,0] vibration_deg, vibration_hz Sinusoidal angular amplitude 0..5 degrees and frequency 0..1000 Hz; defaults 0.03, 80 vibration_phase_deg -360..360 degrees; default 0 samples Odd integer 1..65 maximum temporal samples; default 7; stationary cases use one. Moving cases target 0.5 px spacing, capped here; compare convergence for long exposures height_override_m null (default, use flight AGL), or 0.1..10000 metres; non-null requires a map cache jpeg_quality Integer 1..100; default 95; lossy JPEG encoding follows rendering vignetting Residual linear-light loss at a corner, 0..0.95; default 0 (off); cos-fourth falloff shape optical_blur_px Gaussian optical blur sigma in output pixels, 0..5; default 0 (off), applied in linear light sensor_full_well_e Effective full-well electrons, 10..1,000,000, or 0 (default, noise off). Controls Gaussian shot-noise approximation, not a measured RAW sensor capacity sensor_read_noise_e Effective RMS read noise in electrons, 0..100; default 0; positive values require full well enabled isp_sharpen Luma-only unsharp-mask amount, 0..3; default 0 (off); fixed 1 px Gaussian radius max_tiles Integer 1..225 for the complete projected tile rectangle; default 121 threads Integer 1..32 requested workers; default 4, further restricted by available resources memory_budget_mb Integer 96..1024 MiB working-set budget; default 192, further restricted by available resources f_number 0.5..64, default 1.79; metadata only, not a depth-of-field/diffraction model focal_length_mm null (default) or 0.1..1000 mm; metadata only; projection uses field of view

Calibration coefficients follow OpenCV Brown and fisheye conventions. Projection assumes a centred principal point and a fixed nadir mount. Calibrate the lens, crop, and saved-image mode together; the stock AI Camera profile's nominal field of view does not measure distortion, readout, or aircraft vibration. The profile JSON is not a PANGEA camera INI or an ONNX assignment.

docs.title: Realism Boundary
docs.text:
The renderer integrates motion/exposure in linearized sRGB and then re-encodes JPEG. Time zero is the shot pose at the centre row's mid-exposure. Translation uses the photo's speed/course/AGL; angular rates and sinusoidal vibration are configured, not inferred from neighbouring IMU samples. Brightness is relative EV, not sensor RAW radiometry. Optional residual shading, Gaussian optical softness, signal-dependent shot/read noise, sRGB encoding and luma sharpening approximate the saved camera JPEG, not the actual Bayer sensor/libcamera ISP. Noise is deterministic for the same effective profile and shot metadata, independent of worker count; changed shot metadata changes the seed. Saturated highlights clip. No autoexposure, automatic white balance, Bayer demosaicing, spatial denoising, physical depth of field, weather, buildings, or terrain-height reconstruction is included. The cache itself already contains an aerial image's imaging/compression effects.

Use paired captures and held-out real-flight JPEGs to validate geometry, ground sampling, blur, shutter skew, colour, compression, and model performance. An attractive simulated photo is not evidence that the neural-network domain gap is closed. Preserve the effective profile and its EXIF SHA-256 with results.

docs.title: Calibrate Against Real Captures
docs.text:
The supplied AIcam profile matches USHER's saved 2028x1520, quality 90, 4:2:0 JPEG format (see the AIcam capture guide). Its optical distortion, readout, noise and ISP values are nominal, not measurements. No real AIcam flight-photo calibration is supplied.

  1. Collect real photos in the actual capture mode, with representative lighting, speed, height and terrain. Keep a separate held-out flight.
  2. Calibrate FOV/distortion using OpenCV camera calibration. Measure rolling readout, exposure and vibration independently; photo statistics alone cannot recover them.
  3. Generate matching simulated views and compare batches:
./bin/camera_lens --measure /data/real-flight/*.jpg > /tmp/real-camera.json
./bin/camera_lens --measure /data/sim-flight/*.lens.jpg > /tmp/sim-camera.json

This works on ordinary JPEGs without MIMIC EXIF. JSON contains per-file values and medians: dimensions, estimated IJG JPEG quality, luma mean and 1st/99th percentiles (0..255), flat-region noise sigma (luma levels), Laplacian variance (detail), corner/centre luma ratio, and R/G and B/G. jpeg_table_error=0 means an exact standard IJG luma quantization table; vendor tables give an approximation. Colour subsampling is reported per file. Saturated-only images without usable noise samples are explicitly rejected. Undefined ratios are null and excluded from their batch median. 4. Tune optical_blur_px and isp_sharpen for detail, then effective full well/read noise for flat-region grain, vignetting for residual shading, and exposure_ev/jpeg_quality for brightness/compression. Higher full well reduces noise. Disable each optional effect with 0. To disable the whole emulator in LOOM use LOOM_CAMERA_PROFILE=none. 5. Record the camera mode, conditions, measurements and date in calibration. Validate the profile, restart with fresh LOOM references, and evaluate held-out real-flight neural results before calling the profile representative.

Noise, sharpness, colour and corner ratios are scene-dependent diagnostics, not automatic calibration or proof of a domain match. Use comparable terrain and uniform targets for shading/noise; avoid fitting texture as sensor noise. White-balance differences require matching the real capture/model preprocessing; this profile does not provide a colour-calibration matrix.

docs.title: Performance and Validation
docs.text:
Rendering uses bounded strips and a bounded tile cache. A nonblocking job lock prevents concurrent renderers from multiplying their working sets. The budget is a conservative renderer estimate, not a whole-system RAM guarantee. No Python runtime is required for emulation or LOOM inference.

Each successful render prints elapsed_s, process_peak_rss_kib, effective_threads, effective_samples, estimated_peak_bytes, and center_translation_blur_px_level_estimate. exposure_blur_px_max estimates motion from nine image probes; ray_grid_step_px and ray_interpolation_error_px report the green/reference channel's node spacing and maximum cell-centre forward-reprojection residual. Each colour grid halves its spacing until that residual is at most 0.02 px, or uses exact per-pixel inversion. This is a sampled accuracy check, not a mathematical bound everywhere. Measure at the actual JPEG resolution, flight AGL, speed, and widest required view. In LOOM, rendering finishes before reference admission/inference; slow rendering can reduce the 3-second flight-plan photo cadence. The shared launcher cancels on owner shutdown or after 90 seconds; this limit does not promise real-time operation.

On the development PC, the supplied full-effect AIcam profile rendered a 2028x1520 clean MIMIC source into a 2028x1520 q90 JPEG in 0.13..0.14 s (warm-cache runs including EXIF and fsync, eight workers, about 77 MiB peak process RSS). The 160-degree fisheye profile (spanning 35 zoom-18 tiles) took 0.16..0.18 s at 2028x1520 with about 79 MiB peak process RSS. Both used five effective exposure samples; the AIcam reference-grid residual was 0.0161 px. These are renderer-only host measurements on cached real aerial tiles, not complete flight-cadence, MORA, or real-camera accuracy guarantees.

Reduce temporal samples (odd values only) after checking convergence, or disable unneeded chromatic aberration to avoid three independent colour-ray passes. Do not lower resolution or remove measured effects solely to obtain a favourable timing number. Keep enough cached terrain for the entire distorted, moving footprint; missing imagery fails rather than filling neural inputs with invented terrain.

docs.title: When Emulation Fails
docs.text: Check that the source is a supported clean MIMIC photo, the profile parses, its pose/height information is available, and the cache covers the wider view. Read SODA's error rather than assuming the clean image was used as a quiet fallback. Preserve the original while adjusting the profile.

docs.title: Camera Speed Test
docs.text: Measure completed still-image throughput with USHER's built-in --speedtest. It uses the selected camera backend, retains its photographs and exits. There is no separate speed-test executable to install.

docs.title: Prepare The Target
docs.text:
Build on the development PC and follow deployment to install the current ARM64 release on MORA. Never compile on MORA. For a PC-attached camera, build with make native and run from the checkout instead. Use the camera's normal settings, output storage and connection. Ensure enough free disk space for eleven images per run and any configured companion files.

Only one process may own the camera and USHER endpoint. On MORA, connect over SSH, note whether usher.service is active, and stop it before testing:

ssh air@theatre.local
systemctl is-active usher.service
sudo -n systemctl stop usher.service
cd /home/air/sensoraia

Use the actual host and installation directory. If sudo requires a password, authenticate directly in your terminal; never put the password into a command or log. Stop any other manually started camera owner too.

docs.title: Run A Test
docs.text:
Choose exactly one real image backend:

./usher --lwircam --speedtest
./usher --aicam --speedtest
./usher --aicam --native-photo --speedtest
./usher --spottercam --speedtest
./usher --spottercam --native-photo --speedtest
./usher --chdk --speedtest

Run only the command for your connected camera. No flight controller or UART connection is needed. Do not combine this mode with daemon/local simulation, mock images, EARcam, pose logging or LWIR processing options. The worker's normal settings still apply, so record the settings used for comparisons. The two --native-photo commands use the same direct libcamera capture and do not load or run an object-recognition model. Plain --aicam uses the OS camera tool, while plain --spottercam uses its configured detector. Set USHER_AI_CAM_TIMING=1 to report native frame-acquisition and JPEG-save times separately on standard error.

Capture a log without adding terminal backpressure to the benchmark:

./usher --lwircam --speedtest > /tmp/lwir-speedtest.log 2>&1
result=$?
cat /tmp/lwir-speedtest.log
printf 'exit=%s\n' "$result"

Require exit status zero and ten successful measured captures. Initialization is reported separately; one additional warm-up capture is excluded. Each run uses a new speedtest-* subdirectory under the backend's normal photo root, printed in the final report. Original images are retained, not overwritten. Inspect the saved JPEGs; the benchmark checks the returned path and nonempty regular file, not complete JPEG decoding or temperature-layer correctness.

Repeat several times to distinguish repeatable throughput from a lucky frame boundary. Keep all results, including failures, rather than reporting only the fastest run. On Raspberry Pi, record vcgencmd get_throttled, vcgencmd measure_temp, free -h and the output filesystem alongside the application versions and camera settings.

docs.title: Interpret The Report
docs.text:
Report Meaning Practical sustained speed Ten sequential captures divided by elapsed sequence time, including between-call overhead Average camera-call speed Ten divided by the sum of timed backend calls Average / fastest / slowest capture time Latency distribution over those ten calls Fastest single capture Best individual call; its reciprocal is not demonstrated sustained throughput Initialization Camera preparation before the warm-up; excluded from the rate

Backend-call timing includes the work required by that backend to return a saved image, including encoding/storage where performed there. UART traffic, the normal flight-trigger loop, USHER EXIF/SODA processing and initialization are not part of that number. The sustained interval includes between-call validation/publication work, except work following the final timed return. Do not treat this short benchmark as an endurance or whole-board headroom test.

The Tiny1-C supplies a 25 fps stream, but fresh-request still capture plus durable publication can deliver fewer saved images per second. Kernel frame timestamps are not independently validated exposure timestamps. See LWIRcam for startup, freshness, JPEG quality and exact temperature preservation.

docs.title: Measured AI Camera Example
docs.text:
On 2026-11-01, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W MORA and its connected IMX500 were tested with temporary ARM64 binaries and rpicam-still unavailable on the process PATH. Each run saved ten measured 2028x1520 photographs after one excluded warm-up. Both native selections used the same quality-90 4:2:0 IJG JPEG path, without a detector model.

Native Selection Run 1 Photos/s Run 2 Photos/s Run 3 Photos/s --aicam --native-photo 1.190 1.189 1.190 --spottercam --native-photo 1.190 1.190 1.190

All 66 JPEGs decoded at the expected dimensions; their sensor-frame sequences and timestamps increased within each run. No detection sidecars were produced. The board reported throttled=0x0 before and after, with temperatures of 36.5 and 39.7 C. USHER was restored afterward. This is a short capture test, not an endurance or complete flight-processing measurement.

Earlier on the same board, three plain --aicam runs using rpicam-still measured 2.105, 2.121 and 2.103 photos/s. That path used the tool's quality-93 default and zero-shutter-lag mode, so the two results do not isolate camera access alone: their capture and JPEG pipelines differ.

docs.title: Measured MORA Example
docs.text:
On 2026-10-30, the current ARM64 release was deployed to theatre, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W Rev 1.0, and tested with the real Tiny1-C. Five independent ./usher --lwircam --speedtest runs completed all 50 measured captures plus five excluded warm-ups. USHER was stopped for the tests and restored afterward.

Run Sustained Photos/s Mean Camera Call, ms 1 8.255 121.103 2 8.387 119.184 3 8.427 118.612 4 8.464 118.102 5 8.402 118.977

The best observed sustained rate was 8.464 saved photos/s, about 118 ms per image. The fastest individual call across these runs was 103.883 ms; its reciprocal, 9.626 photos/s, is not a sustained result. Initialization was 3.28-3.39 seconds and excluded, as was the extra warm-up capture.

The worker used native V4L2, bundled IJG JPEG, default quality 95 and 4:4:4 sampling, with native inference settings (no model analysis or mock input). Images were saved to the board's normal microSD-backed ext4 root filesystem, under /home/air/Pictures/sensoraia/. No extra raw companions or statistics were requested. Durable publication remained enabled. The board reported throttled=0x0 before and after, with temperatures of 46.2 and 45.6 C. All 55 JPEGs were subsequently decoded and their embedded 256x192 temperature layers validated on the PC; each contained 49,152 valid temperature samples. No raw companions were retained, so this is not an independent raw-byte comparison. This is a short board-backed throughput observation, not an absolute hardware maximum, endurance test or thermal-accuracy qualification.

Board logs are retained at /home/air/lwir-speedtest-20261030-dFvUqFOE/; the logs identify each image directory. A development-PC evidence copy also retains all images and validation output.

docs.title: Restore The Service
docs.text:
If the service was active before testing, restart it even after a failed test:

sudo -n systemctl start usher.service
systemctl --no-pager --full status usher.service
journalctl -u usher.service -n 30 --no-pager

Leave a previously inactive service inactive. Retain the logs and image paths with the tested release before removing any benchmark output.

docs.title: Use A Canon Camera With CHDKbridge
docs.text:
CHDKbridge lets USHER request photographs and supported controls from a Canon camera over USB. CHDK runs inside the camera; CHDKbridge runs on MORA or your PC. You need both—CHDK loaded on the camera's SD card and CHDKbridge on the host—for this camera path.

Canon-camera terms | Capture with USHER

docs.title: Prepare The Camera
docs.text:
Obtain a stable, non-beta CHDK v1.6 build matching the exact camera model and Canon firmware revision. Sensoraia does not install CHDK, prepare the SD card or replace the camera's firmware for you.

  • Supported cameras
  • Downloads and build selection
  • CHDK 1.6 manual
  • Prepare an SD card

Verify that CHDK loads after a power cycle and that the camera can save a normal JPEG. Leave CHDK's USB Remote shutter-switch feature disabled; it is different from USB/PTP control.

  • Firmware
  • Interesting other library

docs.title: Take Your First Photo
docs.text:
Build on the development PC. Stop USHER and other camera owners before a standalone bench capture, connect a USB data cable and provide reliable power.

make -j32 chdkbridge
bin/chdkbridge --list
bin/chdkbridge --info
bin/chdkbridge photo-001.jpg

Use a new filename in a writable directory. Open the saved JPEG and check focus and exposure. Ordinary capture saves the original on the camera's SD card and downloads it. Existing destination files are not overwritten.

On MORA, deployment installs 99-chdkbridge.rules, which gives the plugdev group (and so the USHER service) access to Canon cameras in PTP mode. If a desktop has mounted the camera, CHDKbridge releases that mount when it starts.

If several cameras are connected, use the port printed by --list:

bin/chdkbridge --port 1-3 photo-002.jpg

The example port is not universal. USB bus/device addresses can change after reconnecting; verify the selected device each time.

docs.title: Choose Settings Deliberately
docs.text:
Unspecified standalone settings are left unchanged. Set only the options your camera supports, and inspect a real photo after changing them:

bin/chdkbridge --iso-mode 400 --flash 2 --resolution 0 --quality 0 photo-003.jpg
Option Meaning --iso-mode Camera ISO-mode property; supported values depend on the model --flash 2 Flash off --resolution 0 Usually the largest image; confirm your camera's mapping --quality 0 Requested superfine JPEG quality where supported --date-stamp 0 Date stamp off --configure Apply supplied settings without taking a photo

Readback errors can leave earlier settings changed. Check the camera before retrying rather than assuming the whole operation was rolled back.

docs.title: Focus And Exposure
docs.text:
Start with autofocus and verify sharpness. For a camera that supports the requested mode, examples include:

bin/chdkbridge --focus-mode af photo-af.jpg
bin/chdkbridge --focus-mode manual --focus-distance inf photo-infinity.jpg
bin/chdkbridge --shutter 1/1000 --iso-real 400 photo-exposure.jpg

Manual/infinity focus, adjustable aperture and ND-filter controls depend on the camera. A successful distance/property readback does not establish image sharpness or actual exposure quality. Do not choose infinity merely because the aircraft will fly; measure the useful focus for your optics and scene.

--iso-mode is not the same as a real-sensitivity override. Use --help for supported alternatives and ranges rather than combining conflicting exposure options. Save comparison photographs before choosing a mission setup.

docs.title: Zoom
docs.text:
bin/chdkbridge zoom 0
bin/chdkbridge zoom 128
bin/chdkbridge zoom 255

These are separate commands. Zero is the wide end and 255 the tele end of the normalized optical range. The middle value is not a guaranteed 2x ratio. Zoom does not take a photo, and changing it can require a fresh focus check.

docs.title: Powered Lens Retraction
docs.text:
bin/chdkbridge --retract-lens

This requests playback mode without powering the camera off. To request prompt retraction on cameras offering the setting, select Lens Retraction: 0 sec in Canon's menu. Confirm the physical lens has retracted: playback confirmation alone does not measure its position. A later capture can extend it again.

docs.title: Keep The Camera Awake
docs.text:
bin/chdkbridge --configure --keep-awake 1

This changes CHDK's idle-shutdown policy to Always; --keep-awake 0 selects Never, not restoration of an earlier intermediate setting. It consumes power and cannot prevent low-battery shutdown or wake an already powered-off camera. Omitting the option leaves the setting unchanged.

Check the result without changing anything. This reads CHDK's setting and, when the firmware reports them, battery voltage and temperatures:

bin/chdkbridge --power-status
# idle_shutdown_policy=3; keep_awake=1; battery_mv=3987; optics_c=30; ...

It exits with an error unless the policy is Always, so it suits a pre-flight check. The bridge never powers the camera off or restarts it, and it never resets the USB device when a command ends.

When the camera exposes them, the same read-only report includes zoom_step, focus_mm, focus_mode and af_lock. Focus mode 0 is autofocus and 1 is manual in the bridge's supported property convention. A focus-distance readback alone does not establish sharpness.

USHER applies --keep-awake 1 on every shot by default (see below), so the policy is re-asserted before each exposure and a camera that lost its saved setting is corrected on the next shot. Before flight, charge the battery and run --power-status: no software setting can prevent shutdown from an empty battery or a camera fault.

docs.title: Retrieve A Camera Crash Log
docs.text:
After an unexpected camera shutdown, switch it on without taking another photo. In CHDK's Miscellaneous menu, enable Enable Lua Native Calls? and confirm its prompt. Stop other camera owners before retrieving the log:

bin/chdkbridge --timeout 60 --usb-timeout 5000 --romlog camera-crash.log

This exports Canon's stored ROM crash log to A/ROMLOG.LOG on the camera's SD card and downloads it to a new local file, limited to 64 KiB. It does not enter record mode, shoot, zoom or power off the camera. The native-call permission must be enabled on the camera; the bridge does not change it. Disable that permission again after the diagnostic when it is no longer needed.

Read the log's timestamp, assertion or exception, and task name before repeating the failed capture. A stored log can describe an earlier failure; compare it with the host's USB and capture logs. For manual export instead, use CHDK's Miscellaneous > Debug parameters > Save ROM crash log command.

docs.title: Optional Direct USB Capture
docs.text:
--direct-download requests direct JPEG transfer rather than an SD-saved JPEG. Support depends on the actual CHDK camera port. If unavailable, resolve compatibility or use ordinary capture; do not assume a failed direct request can be replayed without another exposure.

The bridge reports direct JPEG unsupported; USB capture mask=N when the camera port lacks it. The mask is a bit set: 1 JPEG, 2 RAW, 4 YUV. A Canon SX730 HS (CHDK PTP 2.9) reports mask 6, so only RAW and YUV transfers exist and direct JPEG capture is not available on that camera.

docs.title: Use With USHER
docs.text:
To select CHDKbridge as MORA's active camera service, set CAMERA = chdk in camera.conf at the Sensoraia root or pass CAMERA=chdk when deploying:

make mora-deploy CAMERA=chdk MORA_SSH_TARGET=air@theatre.local

See the deployment guide for full MORA verification steps.

docs.title: Choose USHER's Capture Profile
docs.text:
USHER supplies its own capture profile on each shot. A setting left by a standalone command is not necessarily what USHER will use. For example, select the Canon ISO-mode request while packaging on the PC:

make -j32 mora-package USHER_CHDK_ISO_MODE=400

Keep this choice consistent when rebuilding. The default ISO request is 1600 and the default JPEG quality is 2 (normal). Related settings include USHER_CHDK_FLASH and USHER_CHDK_QUALITY. Confirm supported values and actual photos on your camera; the mode number alone is not measured exposure. Packaging does not activate the service.

The ISO request is applied only when the camera's mode dial is in P, Tv, Av or M. In AUTO and scene modes Canon chooses ISO itself and does not accept a user value; forcing one there made the SX730 HS exposure driver assert (DegeenGain.c in its crash log) and power off when shooting zoomed in dim light. CHDKbridge therefore leaves ISO to the camera in those modes and still applies the other settings. Set the dial to P if you want the configured ISO. On the SX730 HS, ISO 3200 at a zoomed position also powered the camera off, so check any value above 1600 on your own camera.

docs.title: Increase The Shot Rate
docs.text:
For the SX730 HS, start with Canon Image Review: Off, flash off and CHDK RAW saving off. Disable continuous/servo AF when using a focus lock. Image review is a camera-menu setting here, not an option applied by CHDKbridge. These settings remove avoidable camera work; their timing benefit has not been measured on this setup.

The largest measured improvement is JPEG compression, without changing resolution, which is why USHER uses quality 2 (normal) by default. In standalone SX730 captures on MORA, resolution 0 with quality 0 (superfine) produced roughly 8.4--10.5 MB files in 4.85--5.3 s once warm; quality 2 produced roughly 2.8--3.9 MB files in 2.7--3.1 s at the wide end and about 1.9 MB in 3.4--3.5 s zoomed to zoom 128 indoors. These are scene-dependent capture-and-download times, not a guaranteed flight cadence. Normal quality loses some fine detail through stronger compression; inspect small features before relying on it for mapping or detection. To keep superfine JPEGs instead:

make -j32 mora-package USHER_CHDK_QUALITY=0

Packaging alone does not deploy it. Keep the setting on subsequent builds. Do not probe other resolution codes: the SX730 HS uses 0 (L), 2 (M1), 3 (M2) and 5 (S), and an unsupported code ended in a USB disconnect.

To compare fixed focus, with no other camera owner:

bin/chdkbridge --usb-timeout 5000 --focus-mode auto --focus-distance inf photo-focus.jpg

Here auto selects the CHDK port's supported manual-focus or AF-lock distance mechanism; it does not request autofocus. Unsupported modes or rejected distance readback fail explicitly. Check sharpness at the intended zoom and subject distance. If the comparison succeeds, carry it into USHER using USHER_CHDK_FOCUS_MODE=auto USHER_CHDK_FOCUS_DISTANCE=inf on the packaging command. Recheck after zoom changes; fixed infinity focus measured about 0.2 s faster per wide-angle shot on the bench but has not been checked zoomed.

M or Tv mode and a suitable short shutter time can limit exposure time and motion blur, but do not eliminate all camera processing. Lower ISO is not inherently faster: in dim light it may require a longer exposure. Select daylight white balance for consistent color when appropriate; no measured speed gain is established here. The existing --shutter and ISO overrides are available for comparison, but should not replace a correctly exposed photo with a dark one merely to shorten capture time.

USHER overlaps CHDK metadata writing with the next capture. The camera/USB capture lane is still single-flight, so triggers faster than capture and download can finish are not guaranteed to produce photos. Direct JPEG USB capture is unavailable on this SX730 port; it is not a speed option here.

On a camera whose CHDK port supports direct JPEG capture, USHER can ask the bridge for it instead of saving to the SD card first:

make -j32 mora-package USHER_CHDK_DIRECT=1

The default is 0 (SD-saved capture). USHER does not fall back to the other mode when direct capture fails, because that would expose twice.

Every shot also carries --keep-awake 1 (CHDK "Always" idle-shutdown prevention). Select USHER_CHDK_KEEP_AWAKE=0 to request Never, or USHER_CHDK_KEEP_AWAKE= (empty) to leave the camera's own setting alone.

With no other camera owner, a separately managed bench session uses:

./usher --chdk --debug

Do not run standalone CHDKbridge commands while USHER owns the camera. For mission controls use the camera-control guide.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check No camera Power, USB data cable and the selected port Camera busy Desktop photo importers or another camera owner CHDK/protocol rejected Exact camera firmware and stable CHDK build Setting rejected Your camera's supported values and current state Timeout after capture Inspect the camera and destination before deciding whether to request another photo Blurred JPEG Focus, zoom, exposure duration, vibration and real scene detail

When an earlier run was interrupted (stopped, timed out or unplugged), the camera can still hold that run's PTP session or unsent data. CHDKbridge then prints Recovering camera PTP state left by an earlier run, sends the still-image class reset once and opens a fresh session; it never resets the USB port. Likewise it waits for a camera script left running by an interrupted run instead of killing it. USHER removes partial cNNNNNN.jpg.part.* downloads left in the photo directory by a forcibly stopped controller. A camera that has powered off still needs to be switched on again.

Keep usable originals and the diagnostic. A successful build or USB reply does not replace a bench check of the actual camera configuration.

docs.title: Recover Before Requesting Another Photo
docs.text:
A timeout after triggering can mean the exposure succeeded but transfer or confirmation failed. Check the camera's SD card and output directory before repeating it. If you know the saved camera path, download the existing JPEG without another exposure:

bin/chdkbridge --download A/DCIM/100CANON/IMG_0042.JPG recovered.jpg

Use the actual camera filename and a new local destination, with --port when needed. Do not delete originals or kill an unrelated camera script to force recovery. Once the camera is idle and the connection healthy, a new independent capture can be requested.

docs.title: Chemical Vapors and Emissions
docs.text: There is more to a landscape than a camera can show. With the right onboard sensors, a drone can sample carbon dioxide in the air, look for methane leaks, or survey radiation emitted from the ground. It is another way to explore a place: not just what it looks like, but what is happening around it. Pair the readings with the aircraft's position and time, and an invisible change becomes something you can follow, compare and investigate, whether you are checking a biogas installation, studying air quality or looking for an unusual emission.

docs.title: Ten Things A Drone Can Detect
docs.text:
Each example needs a suitable sensor; no single instrument detects everything in this list.

  1. Carbon dioxide (CO2). Measure changes around combustion sources, industrial processes or natural releases with an infrared gas sensor.
  2. Methane (CH4). Look for leaks from gas infrastructure, landfills or biogas facilities with a methane-sensitive instrument.
  3. Carbon monoxide (CO). Detect this combustion gas in smoke or exhaust using an appropriate gas sensor.
  4. Ammonia (NH3). Check for releases around livestock buildings, fertilizer handling or industrial refrigeration.
  5. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S). Detect a gas associated with wastewater, decomposing organic material and some industrial operations.
  6. Sulfur dioxide (SO2). Investigate emissions from sulfur-containing fuels, industrial processes or volcanic activity.
  7. Nitrogen dioxide (NO2). Study a combustion-related air pollutant found in traffic and industrial exhaust.
  8. Volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Screen for groups of vapors from fuels, paints and solvents. Identifying an individual compound needs a more selective instrument or analysis.
  9. Airborne particles, such as dust and smoke. Measure particle levels with an optical particle sensor; particles are not gases or vapors.
  10. Gamma radiation. Survey radiation levels with a dedicated detector. A suitable gamma spectrometer can also help identify radioactive materials.

docs.title: Different Signals, Different Sensors
docs.text:
For many gas measurements, a small pump draws air past a sensor on the aircraft. Other instruments use light to detect particular gases along a viewing path. Radiation sensing is different: the detector measures radiation reaching it, not the smell or chemical makeup of an air sample. A normal camera or thermal imager does not replace these specialist instruments.

Wind moves and dilutes a gas plume, and propeller airflow can change the air reaching an inlet. Sensor placement, response time and calibration therefore matter just as much as where the drone flies. For radiation surveys, distance, shielding, background levels and measurement time affect what can be detected. A higher reading is a useful clue, not automatically the source location or the amount being released.

docs.title: Bringing A New Sensor To Sensoraia
docs.text:
Gas, particle and radiation payloads need their own compatible connection and Sensoraia integration; these are not ready-to-use sensor backends included with the camera and microphone modules. The aim is familiar: keep each reading with its units, measurement time and flight context, so it can become a useful part of an airborne sensing workflow.

Explore Sensoraia's current sensors or see how the autopilot link connects airborne observations to the rest of a mission.

docs.title: Explore Real-World Examples
docs.text: At the moment there is not yet a sensor module in this class but if you need it now then add code andd behaviour to make it a reallity. We look froward to integrate a new class of sensor create by you into Sensoraia. Please make a pull request if you feel you are ready to share it with the world.

docs.title: Laptop To MORA Desk Test
docs.text:
Run the simulated aircraft on the laptop and real USHER on MORA. The FTDI cable supplies 5 V power and carries camera requests/replies over a 3.3 V UART. Start with a mock photo on the board, then use the real camera.

PC demo setup | Prepare the reference Pi board

docs.title: 1. Connect Power And UART
docs.text:
Make connections while unpowered. Use the cable's 5 V power lead and 3.3 V UART signals; those voltages have different jobs.

FTDI Lead Pi Zero 2 W Reference Pin And Purpose 5 V Pin 2, 5 V; power MORA and its camera GND Pin 6, GND; common ground TXD Pin 10, GPIO15 / RXD; laptop sends to MORA RXD Pin 8, GPIO14 / TXD; MORA replies to laptop

Check connector labels, not assumed wire colours—adapter makers treat wire colours as creative expression, and feeding 5 V into a 3.3 V GPIO pin ends the bench test faster than intended. Never connect the 5 V lead to TXD/RXD or the Pi's 3.3 V pin. Connect the camera ribbon while MORA is off, then plug the FTDI cable into the laptop. Keep a real flight controller disconnected for this simulated-aircraft exercise.

MORA needs the installed release, matching sensor runtime and configured UART. Both ends use 115200 baud. Wi-Fi/SSH starts programs and retrieves files; the FTDI UART carries the camera protocol, not an SSH login.

docs.title: 2. Choose The Laptop Port
docs.text:
On the laptop:

ls -l /dev/serial/by-id/

Use your adapter's stable by-id path, or its actual device such as /dev/ttyUSB0. The laptop account needs serial access, normally through dialout on Debian/Ubuntu.

Stop the previous local session. The example launcher automatically prefers a connected MORA cable and skips local sensor companions. Hardware sessions pin both NPS endpoints to that cable; startup refuses a leftover /tmp/usher-sim instead of silently testing the PC. Do not run a serial monitor on the FTDI port.

docs.title: 3. Prepare NPS For The Cable
docs.text:
Use your working fixed-wing NPS aircraft and the public setup. From the Sensoraia root:

export PAPARAZZI_HOME="$HOME/paparazzi"
./kickstart.sh
make -C "$PAPARAZZI_HOME" -f Makefile.ac AIRCRAFT=Easystar_3_SPOTTERCAM nps.compile

By default, the nps transport uses /dev/ttyUSB0 whenever no local PC /tmp/usher-sim peer is running. If several USB-serial adapters are attached, pass MORA_UART_DEVICE=/dev/serial/by-id/usb-FTDI_... via DIGITAL_CAM_UART_FALLBACK_DEVICE="$MORA_UART_DEVICE" on the make command above (after removing var/aircrafts/Easystar_3_SPOTTERCAM/nps/modules/digital_cam/uart_cam_ctrl.o). This photo-survey plan requests the AI camera slot; USHER on MORA selects whether to capture a mock or physical image.

Start Paparazzi Center:

cd "$PAPARAZZI_HOME"
./paparazzi

Select userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_conf.xml, aircraft Easystar_3_SPOTTERCAM (or your own configured aircraft) and nps (click Build if you have not built nps yet). Choose userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_control_panel.xml and Sensoraia MORA desk NPS. This session starts Simulator, Data Link, Server and PprzGCS, with no local sensor peer, so nps connects straight to MORA over the FTDI cable.

docs.title: 4. Check Real UART With A Mock Photo
docs.text:
In another laptop terminal, connect to MORA over SSH and run foreground USHER against /dev/serial0:

ssh -t air@theatre.local 'sudo systemctl stop usher.service && cd /home/air/sensoraia && ./usher --serial /dev/serial0 --aicam --test --debug; status=$?; sudo systemctl start usher.service; exit $status'

Substitute your MORA SSH target (air@theatre.local) and installation path (/home/air/sensoraia). The command stops the managed service, runs foreground USHER over SSH and restores usher.service after the foreground command ends.

If you prefer running each step interactively in an SSH terminal on MORA:

sudo systemctl stop usher.service
cd /home/air/sensoraia
./usher --serial /dev/serial0 --aicam --test --debug

Use your actual installation path. End foreground USHER with Ctrl+C when finished, then run sudo systemctl start usher.service. Do not leave the managed service and foreground program competing for the UART or camera.

docs.title: Optional: Full Hands-Free Automation With /home/air/pass.txt
docs.text:
If you want completely hands-free deployment (make mora-deploy) and SSH desk testing with zero password typing, you can place your MORA account's sudo password in /home/air/pass.txt on MORA (replacing replacewithyourpass with your actual password) and lock its permissions to owner-only (chmod 600):

ssh air@theatre.local 'umask 077 && printf "%s\n" "replacewithyourpass" > ~/pass.txt && chmod 600 ~/pass.txt'

Edit ~/pass.txt on MORA so it contains your real sudo password (the literal placeholder replacewithyourpass is safely ignored until you change it). deploy_mora.sh automatically detects ~/pass.txt on MORA and authenticates sudo without prompting. You can also start and restore foreground bench runs directly from your PC in one line:

ssh air@theatre.local 'sudo -S -p "" systemctl stop usher.service < /home/air/pass.txt && cd /home/air/sensoraia && exec ./usher --chdk --debug'

After the foreground process exits, restore the managed service:

ssh air@theatre.local 'sudo -S -p "" systemctl start usher.service < /home/air/pass.txt'

Wait for USHER to report /dev/serial0 and readiness. Start the Center desk session, wait for live telemetry/GPS, then select Takeoff. Watch requests arrive on MORA and mock JPEGs complete during the survey. Do not use --local on MORA: the physical UART is the point of this step.

docs.title: 5. Change To The Physical Camera
docs.text:
Stop the desk session and end foreground USHER with Ctrl+C before changing the backend. With the AI Camera prepared:

ssh -t air@theatre.local 'sudo systemctl stop usher.service && cd /home/air/sensoraia && ./usher --serial /dev/serial0 --aicam --debug; status=$?; sudo systemctl start usher.service; exit $status'

Repeat the desk flight. Without --test, this uses actual camera exposures. Other sensors need their corresponding camera mask and mission selection, not just a different backend flag.

The desk session checks UART/capture operation. It does not run the PC T1..T5 ranking companion. Physical pixels paired with simulated pose do not measure real-flight geolocation accuracy.

docs.title: Inspect Results And Finish
docs.text:
For the default account, in another laptop terminal:

ssh air@theatre.local 'ls -lt ~/Pictures/sensoraia/ | head'

Use the actual output directory printed by USHER. The files are on MORA, not in a PC companion's run directory. Check the new readable JPEG, completion diagnostic and EXIF; a GCS shot marker alone does not prove capture finished.

Let NPS land, stop its session programs and end foreground USHER with Ctrl+C. Check that usher.service is active again. To return to PC-only simulation, disconnect the cable, unset any explicit MORA_UART_DEVICE override, and restart the normal session. An explicitly empty MORA_UART_DEVICE can force PC-only operation while the cable remains connected.

docs.title: If Nothing Arrives
docs.text: Check crossed TX/RX, common ground, serial permissions, the actual laptop device and MORA's disabled serial login console. Check that no local peer is taking precedence and no second application owns a UART. If requests arrive but capture fails, investigate the sensor error rather than rewiring a working link.

docs.title: Diplacam: Choose Where To Measure Next
docs.text:
Diplacam uses measurements already collected to propose eight useful places to sample next. Its map belief tracks both estimated values and uncertainty, so the next proposal can change as new observations arrive.

The supplied experiment samples a numerical field from a CSV. It runs the native planner and selected ONNX model, not a physical full-spectrum-camera driver. Start with the standalone command, then try the rotorcraft simulation.

Planning terms | Paparazzi setup

docs.title: Try A Standalone Plan
docs.text:
From the Sensoraia root:

make -j32 diplacam
bin/diplacam --field modules/dipla_cam/data/map_26_NAIP_grid_counts.csv --east 4 --north 4

The command prints eight slot,east_m,north_m rows. Internal slots 0..7 correspond to P1..P8 in the example. This does not start a flight or move waypoints. Read model/field diagnostics on stderr if planning fails.

docs.title: Choose The Model And Field
docs.text:
The assignment lives in modules/dipla_cam/diplacam_settings.ini. Keep the graph, descriptor and deployment metadata together. Paths are relative to the settings file; --settings selects another assignment.

The current field uses x,y,count CSV rows on a 51-by-51, two-metre grid covering 0..100 m east/north. Only the sensor footprint is sampled into the belief. Unmeasured field truth is not handed to the network as the answer. The supplied profile uses a two-grid-cell flight margin: XY stays within 4..96 m. This also applies to the standalone command's printed points. flight_margin_cells changes that inset for both planners without changing the model grid or the demo height.

The worker INI selects the field, not its geographic location. The flight plan chooses where the aircraft begins the survey; Diplacam anchors the field to its first accepted position. For custom experiments, an absolute field path avoids working-directory ambiguity.

docs.title: Place The Survey
docs.text:
The existing START command arms the survey. Its first valid admitted shot provides the measured latitude/longitude that becomes local (50,50), the centre of the 100-by-100-metre field. Local X increases east and Y increases north. With the supplied two-cell margin, targets span approximately 46 m in each direction from that measured centre.

Paparazzi owns the approach and GPS checks. The supplied Begin survey block flies to CENTRE, waits there at the configured height, and starts Diplacam. Choose that entry waypoint using Paparazzi's normal local or geographic coordinates; its existing relative-waypoint facilities can also position an entry manoeuvre. No geographic origin is duplicated in the worker settings.

The anchor is the accepted shot's actual position, not an assumption that the aircraft is exactly at the waypoint. The mission's area check around CENTRE allows for entry-position error as well as the field extent. Keep that check consistent with the entry location when adapting the mission. HOME and landing geometry remain independent.

Event Geographic Frame And Belief START from stopped Wait for the first valid admitted shot, then capture its position once Another START while active Retain the anchor and belief; request the next eight-point chunk Duplicate or rejected shot Do not establish or move the anchor STOP, then START Start a new survey with a new first-position anchor and belief

Shot numbering does not have to start at one. The existing session token and shot number correlate commands and measurements; they do not replace the flight controller's GPS-validity checks. Before anchoring or before a complete route is ready, replies cannot authorize waypoint updates.

Standalone planning has no geographic frame: --east and --north select an observation directly on the CSV grid and still default to (4,4). To exercise the worker's centred first-observation case with a fresh standalone stream:

bin/diplacam --field modules/dipla_cam/data/map_26_NAIP_grid_counts.csv --east 50 --north 50

docs.title: How The Method Works
docs.text:
A Gaussian Process updates the estimated field and uncertainty from the observed footprint. A learned diffusion model, trained to imitate informative plans, then supports twenty denoising steps that produce eight locations. This is a measurement planner, not an object detector or a motor controller.

Each accepted shot supplies one measurement footprint. Measurements include reproducible Gaussian sensor noise, separate from the diffusion sampler's random stream. They update the GP in order while the aircraft follows its retained route, rather than being replaced by whichever pose arrives last.

The bundled model uses XYZ internally and was trained for 10..40 m heights. The current demo deliberately commands 2 m and uses only predicted XY. Predicted Z never commands altitude. Correct software execution at 2 m does not establish planning quality outside that training range. In the supplied profile, injected noise and GP likelihood both use variance 0.01. The reference's height-dependent law cannot be extrapolated unchanged to 2 m because it would produce a negative variance.

docs.title: Configure An Experiment
docs.text:
Two flat INI files have different responsibilities:

File Purpose Path Base diplacam_settings.ini Model assignment, inference limits, GP, synthetic sensor and comparison policy Paths inside this file are relative to the file Worker INI selected by --config Field, planning cadence and planning-pose age field is relative to the worker's working directory; an absolute path avoids ambiguity

The module supplies a commented diplacam_settings.ini and diplacam-example.ini. Use one key=value per line, no sections, and put comments on separate lines. Unknown or duplicate keys, malformed numbers, nonfinite values and out-of-range settings stop startup instead of silently choosing another experiment.

Inspect the effective application settings without loading a graph, field or ONNX Runtime:

bin/diplacam --show-config
bin/diplacam --settings /absolute/path/experiment.ini --show-config

This reports resolved application paths and defaults, not worker configuration. Both files are read once at process startup. Restart the standalone program or USHER's Diplacam worker to apply edits; requesting another chunk does not reload settings. Standalone and worker planning use the same application snapshot.

docs.title: GP, Sensor And Flight Margin
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning And Accepted Values diffusion_seed 123 Independent sampler seed, unsigned 64-bit integer including zero sensor_noise_seed 149 Independent synthetic measurement-noise seed, same integer range flight_margin_cells 2 Integer 0..24; inset is this value times 2 m on each XY edge gp_prior_mean 0.2 Finite initial field estimate, in field units gp_kernel_variance 0.0079 Positive finite Matern marginal variance, in squared field units gp_lengthscale_m 4.78 Positive finite spatial correlation length, in metres sensor_fov_deg 60 Finite full footprint angle, strictly between 0 and 180 degrees sensor_noise_variance 0.01 Positive finite measurement variance, used for both injected noise and GP likelihood

For example, flight_margin_cells=5 constrains published XY to 10..90 m and also constrains comparison controls. It does not change raw DDIM output, the observation domain or the fixed 2 m mission height. The GP prior mean is independent of cmaes_utility_threshold; changing one does not change the other.

Identical seeds reproduce each stream for the same inputs and call sequence; they do not make differently ordered observations equivalent. A standalone run starts fresh streams. The worker retains both streams and its belief across active START chunk requests. STOP followed by START creates a new survey and resets the sensor stream; the diffusion stream continues until process restart. Rejected duplicate observations consume no sensor noise.

Changing the GP or sensor profile changes the belief presented to the trained model. The graph and its normalization are not retrained by an INI edit. Keep the supplied profile as the reproducible baseline when evaluating changes.

docs.title: Cached Conditioning
docs.text:
An optional matched model bundle computes the map and position conditioning once per route instead of repeating it in all twenty denoising calls. The number of diffusion steps, GP observations, noise and flight-height policy are unchanged. Select it in model settings with:

conditioning_cache=conditioning-cache

The path is relative to the settings file. The bundle must match the original model and contain its verified encoder, denoiser and tensor descriptors. An invalid selected bundle is an error, not a silent fallback. Omitting the setting retains the original sampler; --conditioning-cache DIR selects a bundle for one invocation, while an explicitly empty CLI value disables it.

Releases packaged with this option include both diplacam_cached_settings.ini and diplacam_reference_settings.ini under share/diplacam/. Compare either from the installation root:

bin/diplacam --field share/diplacam/field.csv \
   --settings share/diplacam/diplacam_reference_settings.ini
bin/diplacam --field share/diplacam/field.csv \
   --settings share/diplacam/diplacam_cached_settings.ini

For the managed service, copy the chosen settings over share/diplacam/diplacam_settings.ini and restart usher.service to apply it. Keep the named copies for switching back without rebuilding. A measured Pi Zero 2 W comparison reduced warm inference from about 1.68 seconds to 0.56 seconds. Across sixteen complete test routes, the largest difference from the original sampler was 0.44 mm; the two paths are numerically close, not bit-for-bit identical.

docs.title: Worker Field And Timing
docs.text:
field=/absolute/path/map_26_NAIP_grid_counts.csv
cadence_ms=1000
planning_pose_max_age_ms=1000

Only field is required. Geographic placement is captured from the first valid admitted shot of each survey, not read from this file. The small-field conversion accepts an anchor within absolute 80 degrees latitude and 179.99 degrees longitude; polar and date-line-crossing surveys are not supported.

cadence_ms defaults to 1000, accepts 100..5000, and sets the minimum cooldown after a planning attempt finishes, not a fixed-rate timer, measurement cadence or route-completion rule. Another requested chunk and fresh input are required. planning_pose_max_age_ms defaults to 1000 and accepts 1..5000: an admitted pose must still be this fresh when a new plan starts. An older accepted measurement can update the belief without being eligible to start a plan. Continue providing fresh observations while waiting for a route.

This plan-start age check is separate from the fixed 5000 ms observation/reply lease and the transport's point-cycle timeout. Those remain transport rules, not experiment tuning controls. The fixed model contract also remains 51-by-51 cells over 0..100 m, eight XYZ points, three belief channels and twenty denoising steps. The model's 10..40 m Z normalization does not change the demo's 2 m command height in the original plan. A smaller physical survey uses the explicit frame settings below; the original defaults remain unchanged.

docs.title: Cyberzoo And OptiTrack
docs.text:
