Take the next view under a new name. Copy originals to the laptop without resizing or re-encoding them; copy matching raw companions too if recorded. Do not use mock imagery or display-rotated exports for the real lens fit.

docs.title: 5. Take A Useful Set Of Photos
docs.text:
Collect at least 15 usable fitting views with varied tilt, position, distance and in-plane rotation. Let corners visit the image edges as well as the centre. Keep the full grid visible, flat and sharp.

Set aside 5-8 genuinely new views for checking. Do not fit with those same images or delete difficult views merely to improve a score. Replace an image only when you can identify its problem, and retain your reason.

docs.title: 6. Fit The Lens On The Laptop
docs.text:
The native calibration application runs on the development PC. Build it from the Sensoraia root; the project reuses its static OpenCV calibration modules and bundled JPEG codec, so no separate calibration package is needed:

make -j"$(nproc)" lwir_calibrate

Keep fitting photos in calibration/photos, independent checks in calibration/check and mounting views in calibration/mount. Then run:

bin/lwir_calibrate lens \
  --images calibration/photos --check calibration/check \
  --columns 7 --rows 6 --square-mm 50 \
  --output calibration/tiny1c-lens.yml

The normal ARM64 build also creates a MORA-compatible copy, included in the release package for optional manual calibration work. It is not started by the USHER service, and packaging does not upload or activate it:

make -j"$(nproc)" arm64
bin/lwir_calibrate-arm64 --help
make -j"$(nproc)" mora-package MORA_INSTALL_DIR=/home/air/sensoraia

The package is assembled on the development PC; deployment is a separate command. The utility remains a standalone tool and is not part of USHER's startup command. Use your actual board dimensions and measured pitch. A new output name is required for a separate attempt. Inspect the corner overlays, detected/skipped file list and independent-check errors, not only the summary number.

Reprojection error is in pixels, not metres of GPS error. Correct-looking overlays and comparable independent checks are necessary; no universal RMS threshold guarantees geographic accuracy. A good centre-only fit does not validate the image edges.

docs.title: 7. Measure The Mounting Without Guessing
docs.text:
Secure the aircraft over a horizontal target, using its defined body-axis reference. A convenient fuselage surface may not be that reference. Align board columns with aircraft right and rows toward the tail. Resolve any disagreement between the FC's level reference and the physical datum first.

With the camera in its final bracket:

bin/lwir_calibrate mount \
  --image calibration/mount/mount01.jpg \
  --lens calibration/tiny1c-lens.yml \
  --columns 7 --rows 6 --square-mm 50 \
  --output calibration/tiny1c-mounted.yml

Inspect the numbered corners: 0 is the near-nose, aircraft-left inner corner; 1 is next toward aircraft right; 7 starts the next row toward the tail for this seven-column board. A checkerboard can be detected in the opposite order. Use --reverse-corners only for the identified 180-degree reversal, with a new output name. Do not guess signs or rotations until a result looks plausible.

docs.title: 8. Check Distances Before Checking GPS
docs.text:
Use target positions and distances not used in fitting. Compare predicted directions/ground offsets with measured physical references across the image, including its edges. Recheck with a separately collected set.

For a local geometry check, secure the aircraft over a level patch with propulsion disconnected. Measure camera height and use a plumb line to mark its ground projection. Put independently measured targets forward, right, left and near the usable image edges. Check directions before comparing small distance errors, then repeat with known changed heading/attitude. Use the actual stationary pose/height rather than old flight metadata.

Checkerboard fitting does not require hotspot detection. A checkerboard can correctly produce zero detected hotspots; do not heat a household target dangerously to force a detection. End-to-end hot-target checks need a suitable controlled target. Tape measurements check relative geometry, while absolute GPS error needs an independently surveyed reference and its uncertainty.

A systematic offset suggests mounting/reference error; growing edge error suggests lens or mode mismatch. Before blaming GPS, check the image axes, target geometry, ground plane and observation timing.

Error Pattern Investigate First Grows toward image edges Lens fit, crop or wrong image dimensions Similar offset that rotates with heading Mounting alignment Changes with speed/turn direction Observation timing or motion blur Slowly drifting displacement of every target Position reference or GNSS bias Changes over sloping terrain AGL and the flat-ground assumption

These are clues, not unique diagnoses; change one thing at a time.

docs.title: 9. Install The Profile Deliberately
docs.text:
Retain the original fit and reports. Set verified: 1 only after reviewing the lens, corner ordering, mounting and independent geometry checks. It is a review gate, not certification of GPS or field accuracy.

The runtime profile uses original native dimensions, fitted fx/fy/cx/cy, distortion coefficients and the camera-to-body rotation. Do not substitute a cropped display matrix or pre-undistort the image: the runtime projects the calibrated ray itself.

Copy the reviewed profile to MORA and select it in the actual USHER launch configuration, for example:

--lwir-calibration /home/air/sensoraia/calibration/tiny1c-mounted.yml

Use your installed account/path. Changing a command in an SSH terminal does not update an already running service. Apply configuration changes through the deployment procedure.

To inspect a copy of an existing flight-tagged photo:

bin/lwircam --geolocate calibration/check-shot.jpg \
  --calibration calibration/tiny1c-mounted.yml
exiftool -b -UserComment calibration/check-shot.jpg

The geolocation command updates the JPEG, so work on a copy. Preserve any raw companion too. Missing/unreviewed calibration or unsuitable pose evidence must not be treated as a valid target position. ExifTool is optional inspection software, not a runtime requirement.

docs.title: 10. Keep Temperature Checks Separate
docs.text:
Lens fitting does not calibrate temperature. Begin by checking the camera's existing temperature response rather than replacing factory corrections without evidence.

Use stable references with known uncertainty and suitable surfaces. Allow camera and references to reach a stable condition, record gain/range and repeat measurements at several temperatures. Reflections and emissivity matter: a shiny surface can show reflected surroundings rather than its own temperature.

A contact probe and matte comparison patch can help triage a problem, but are not automatically a traceable absolute-temperature reference. For such claims use suitable calibrated references and include their uncertainty.

If measured corrections are necessary, fit only within the verified camera, gain and range, then test independent intermediate/hold-out references. Keep raw observations and prior results. Do not divide Celsius by emissivity or extrapolate a profile beyond its support range.

docs.title: 11. Check The Whole Flight Measurement
docs.text: Onboard geolocation also depends on aircraft position, real AGL, attitude, mounting, exposure timing and terrain. Compare independent ground targets under representative conditions before relying on a metre-level claim. Simulation, successful fitting and printed decimal places cannot replace that check.

docs.title: 12. Quick Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check Few detected boards Thermal contrast, sharpness, complete pattern and correct corner counts Large edge errors Edge coverage, focus, dimensions and lens model Mount rotated/reversed Physical board axes and numbered corner order Good fit, poor ground locations Mounting, timing, height/reference system and terrain Good geometry, poor temperatures Independent thermal references, gain, emissivity and reflections

docs.title: 13. Save A Reusable Calibration Pack
docs.text: Keep originals, fitting/check sets, board dimensions, overlays, reports, reviewed profiles, camera/mode identity and independent reference results together. If you change the optics or installation, retain the old pack and make a new one rather than silently reusing it.

docs.title: LWIRcam: Capture Thermal Images
docs.text:
LWIRcam saves images from supported USB thermal cameras. With supported Tiny1C data it also retains temperature samples and can measure selected regions. Start with one clean capture before changing rendering or analysis.

Thermal terms | Calibrate your camera

Camera Available Data Tiny1C combined mode 256 x 192 display image and a separate 256 x 192 temperature plane TDK IRcamera 5474:5411 640 x 512 display image; no temperature plane in this supported mode

docs.title: Build On The PC
docs.text:
make -j32 lwircam
bin/lwircam --features

For an ARM64 release use the installation workflow. --features reports the capture backend (capture=v4l2, native Linux V4L2 with the kernel uvcvideo driver) and which optional analysis/mock features are built. The development PC supplies Linux headers; no compiler or development packages are needed on MORA. Hotspot geolocation and ONNX classification need analysis enabled consistently for USHER and its worker, for example LWIR_ENABLE_ANALYSIS=1 when building the selected release. Ordinary image/temperature capture does not require it.

To deploy the full Sensoraia suite on MORA with LWIRcam selected as the active service, set CAMERA = lwircam in camera.conf or run:

make mora-deploy CAMERA=lwircam

Or, to deploy a minimal LWIR-only package (excluding the other camera workers and models):

make mora-deploy MORA_PROFILE=lwircam

Both configure usher.service to start usher --lwircam. For an NPS flight using the physical thermal camera and UART, follow the laptop-to-MORA desk test with aircraft Easystar_3_LWIRCAM (USHER_CAMERA_MASK_LWIR). The connected FTDI cable selects MORA automatically. The capture-only build does not return hotspot navigation points.

docs.title: ARM64 CPU Profiles
docs.text:
The normal ARM64 build targets Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. Select the intended CPU when cross-compiling on the development PC:

make lwircam-arm64 ARM64_BOARD=pi-zero2w
ARM64_BOARD CPU Tuning pi-zero2w Cortex-A53; default for MORA radxa-zero3w Cortex-A55 orange-pi5b Cortex-A76/A55 combination generic Portable ARMv8-A baseline

Choose one profile for the board that will run the binary. Tuned builds are not interchangeable with every ARM64 processor. Rendering and temperature statistics already use native NEON fast paths where supported. CPU tuning does not activate a GPU, hardware JPEG encoder or NPU, and does not qualify a board's OS image or camera drivers. Use a matching target sysroot when required and measure on the actual board. Continue to build on the PC and deploy binaries, not compilers or development packages, to MORA.

Tiny1C's combined stream supplies 25 independent frames per second in the tested mode. Faster processing cannot create additional camera frames. Measure camera wait, rendering, JPEG encoding, metadata and durable storage separately; using more threads is not automatically faster for a 256x192 image. Keep resource headroom for the whole Pi Zero 2 W's shared 512 MB, not only the capture worker.

docs.title: Native V4L2 Capture
docs.text:
Native capture opens only supported USB camera identities and image-capture endpoints, not arbitrary video or metadata devices. Automatic discovery checks /dev/video0 through /dev/video63 and requires exactly one supported image endpoint. Multiple cameras are an error, never an arbitrary first-device choice. Select the actual serial or an actual stable /dev/v4l/by-id/ image-device link:

bin/lwircam --device /dev/v4l/by-id/ACTUAL-CAMERA-IMAGE-LINK \
  --native-raw --stats /absolute/path/native-thermal.jpg

An explicit path can also select a higher-numbered device. If both path and serial are provided, they must identify the same camera. The config key device=/dev/v4l/by-id/ACTUAL-CAMERA-IMAGE-LINK selects the worker device when USHER is given that LWIR config. Device selection is rejected for offline replay.

The driver requires exact YUYV dimensions, tightly packed rows and full frame length. Tiny1C image-only 256x192 negotiation, padded rows, partial/error frames, duplicate/backward sequences and stale qualified monotonic buffers cannot become successful captures. It owns two to four bounded MMAP buffers, requeues each dequeued frame before success and releases partial startup resources on failure. Eight-frame qualification is only for the first startup of a newly seen USB camera instance. It is not repeated for later photos, a quiet interval, rejected frames, a sequence gap, reopen or a worker restart. A private volatile record under /run/lock remembers completion for the service user, keyed to the host boot and USB enumeration identity. The kernel does not expose a sensor power-cycle counter: a genuinely new USB enumeration is treated as new startup. An inaccessible startup record is an explicit error, never a reason to silently repeat the wait.

Later requests select the next usable fresh frame without rebuilding a frame count. Older queued frames are skipped, never returned as that request's photo. Missing, corrupt or neutral-fill frames may still delay capture until valid data arrives; that is not an artificial warmup delay. Optional scene/settling checks still apply when explicitly selected, but never add an eight-frame wait after startup. The configured warmup time also applies only to initial startup. Images are copied only when needed for settling or a selected capture.

Polling is event-driven, with short cancellation intervals and monotonic deadlines; kernel/driver stalls cannot be preempted by a userspace deadline.

Fatal queue/protocol failures block further use of that session until it is closed and reopened. Cleanup retains any mapping the kernel failed to unmap, so a repeated close can release it; reopening cannot overwrite that ownership. Descriptor-close errors are not blindly retried, because Linux may already have released the descriptor number. These checks reduce long-running failure risks; they do not guarantee that a USB cable, camera or kernel driver cannot fail. Validate the intended installation with a sustained soak test before relying on unattended all-day operation.

Real Tiny1C transitions can produce a full-sized neutral fill: every byte pair in both planes is 00 80, displaying black while falsely converting to a uniform 238.85 C. Live capture rejects that exact whole-frame pattern and any entirely invalid temperature plane, and waits for good frames or the existing deadline. A real 0x8000 temperature in a useful frame is not rejected. Offline replay remains structural evidence, not fresh capture.

The supplied service includes the video group and camera-specific video-node udev rules. The kernel uvcvideo driver must be bound, and other camera owners must be stopped; reconnect the device if another USB tool previously detached the kernel driver and the normal video nodes do not reappear. Permission, busy, unplug and driver errors are failures, not permission to use an old frame.

Native --device-state uses Linux USBFS control requests for the existing Tiny1C read-only mailbox protocol. It opens the matched USB node only for the snapshot, verifies the USB-instance identity, and closes it afterward without claiming interfaces or detaching uvcvideo. This requires read/write permission on the USB device node as well as normal video-node access. Image-only TDK still has no temperature/state support.

Host dequeue/arrival time and the kernel's monotonic buffer timestamp/flags are preserved separately. Neither is automatically qualified as exposure time, even when the kernel marks a timestamp as start-of-exposure. The kernel may overwrite buffer metadata during requeue; accepted-frame clock evidence is snapshotted before returning buffer ownership. Revalidate measured latency when changing USB topology or kernel drivers; previous lag measurements must not silently be reused for attitude-sensitive projection. Saved JPEG temperature bytes remain exact and native; the kernel timestamp is additional evidence, not calibration.

LWIRcam captures directly through Linux V4L2 and USBFS, with no external UVC or USB user-space library dependencies. Host fault tests and cross-compilation alone do not qualify a real camera: verify a fresh full-height JPEG, its complete thermal plane and an exact raw companion on the target.

docs.title: First Camera JPEG
docs.text:
Stop other owners of the camera, connect it and use a new filename:

bin/lwircam /absolute/path/first-thermal.jpg

Open the JPEG and check focus, orientation and the expected scene. With multiple devices, choose the actual serial using --serial SERIAL. Permission errors need device-access setup, not repeated captures.

Native Tiny1C capture must report native V4L2 YUYV 256x384 transport, 256x192 image and temperature planes. The 384 transport rows contain the full 192-row image followed by the full 192-row temperature plane, not a cropped or resized sensor image. Its other advertised 256x192 UVC mode is image-only and must never be split into two 96-row planes. LWIRcam rejects that mode and non-native live Tiny1C dimensions. An unoriented JPEG without a legend is 256 x 192; its embedded temperature plane always remains 256 x 192. A raw combined companion is 196608 bytes.

For the TDK mode, preserve the native 640 x 512 dimensions. It is image-only: colourful pixels do not provide temperatures, statistics or thermal calibration.

docs.title: Measurements And Threshold Coverage
docs.text:
These examples require a supported Tiny1C temperature plane:

bin/lwircam --stats /absolute/path/statistics.jpg
bin/lwircam --roi 32 24 128 96 --thresholds 15 45 /absolute/path/region.jpg
bin/lwircam --point 128 96 --average-3x3 /absolute/path/spot.jpg

ROI, point and line coordinates refer to the original sensor image: origin at the top left, X right and Y down. Check the actual native dimensions. Out-of-range selections are rejected rather than silently clipped.

Thresholds specify an inclusive temperature band for diagnostic coverage, not a command to change sensor gain. The printed min/max, averages and coverage describe the selected valid samples; they are not independent temperature calibration. Printed decimal places are not measured accuracy.

docs.title: Display Orientation And Acceleration
docs.text:
bin/lwircam --rotate 90 --mirror /absolute/path/oriented.jpg
bin/lwircam --window 15 45 --palette iron --legend /absolute/path/fixed-window.jpg
bin/lwircam --percentiles 2 98 --palette white-hot /absolute/path/contrast.jpg

Rotation is clockwise, followed by mirror/flip. These change the displayed view, not the raw temperature coordinates. A fixed window makes successive views easier to compare; percentiles emphasize the current scene's contrast. Neither creates additional sensor detail or changes preserved temperatures.

docs.title: Adjust Image Contrast
docs.text:
If the picture looks flat or grey, higher contrast can make small temperature differences easier to see. These software controls draw the JPEG from the temperature plane; they do not change camera gain or temperature calibration. There is no separate --contrast option. Use a new output filename for each capture.

Start with automatic contrast:

bin/lwircam --percentiles 2 98 /absolute/path/contrast.jpg

This spreads the middle 96% of the scene's temperature samples from black to white. The coldest 2% appear black and the hottest 2% appear white. Try --percentiles 5 95 for stronger contrast, with more extremes shown as solid black or white. Automatic contrast adapts to each picture, so the same temperature can have a different brightness in the next picture.

For USHER, add or update these settings in the LWIR config passed with --lwir-config:

percentile_low=2
percentile_high=98
palette=white-hot

For consistent brightness between pictures, use a fixed temperature range instead:

bin/lwircam --window 20 35 /absolute/path/fixed-contrast.jpg

With the default white-hot palette, 20 C becomes black and 35 C becomes white. Temperatures below or above that range also appear black or white. Choose a range that suits the scene. In a USHER config, use window_low_c=20 and window_high_c=35 instead of the two percentile settings. Use either automatic percentiles or a fixed window, not both in the same command or config.

The saved temperature samples stay unchanged, even where the picture becomes solid black or white. Higher contrast adds no sensor detail and does not make temperature readings more accurate. For Spottercam, keep the chosen rendering mode and settings consistent between model training and operation.

docs.title: JPEG Quality And Speed
docs.text:
Use the generic Camera Speed Test to measure saved-image throughput on the deployed board. Sensor frame rate, fastest single capture and sustained saved-image rate are distinct metrics.

Normal captures use JPEG quality 95 with 4:4:4 sampling. It is usually a useful balance between picture detail, file size and encoding work. Quality 100 is also lossy; it is not a way to preserve exact original image pixels. Keep the raw companion when those original bytes are needed.

Select quality 100 for comparison, or set another value from 1 to 100:

bin/lwircam --jpeg-quality 100 /absolute/path/quality-comparison.jpg

For USHER, put jpeg_quality=95 or jpeg_quality=100 in its LWIR config. The command-line option overrides the config for a standalone capture. The selected quality and 4:4:4 sampling are recorded in the JPEG's capture evidence. Existing zero-initialized library callers retain their quality-100 default; the capture worker explicitly selects 95.

The embedded temperature plane remains exact at every JPEG quality. Its 98304 bytes also limit total-file savings: only the displayed image becomes more compressed. Lower quality can soften small details, especially at this sensor resolution. Keep quality, rendering and palette consistent between Spottercam training and operation, and evaluate small-object detection before changing a deployed model's input policy.

A paired development-PC test on the same recorded Tiny1C frame measured about 0.93 ms per JPEG at quality 100 and 0.73 ms at 95, excluding USB and storage. Total file size fell from about 124 kB to 111 kB while all temperature bytes remained identical. These are PC measurements, not Pi or other-board speed claims. File publication still includes synchronization and no-overwrite checks; those safeguards are not removed to inflate throughput. A separate live PC run with raw companions, statistics and durable writes enabled saved about 12.36 photos/s at quality 100 and 12.51 at 95. The encoder's speedup therefore must not be presented as the same percentage gain for the whole capture pipeline.

docs.title: Preserve Raw Measurements
docs.text:
bin/lwircam --native-raw /absolute/path/baseline.jpg

The raw companion is baseline.jpg.raw. Keep it with the JPEG when you need the exact combined frame. The supported thermal JPEG also retains its temperature plane; a screenshot cannot replace it.

For offline replay use --raw with the recorded dimensions and a new output. Replay exercises stored data, not a fresh camera exposure.

For example, for a recorded 256-by-192 Tiny1C combined frame:

bin/lwircam --raw /absolute/path/baseline.jpg.raw --size 256 192 /absolute/path/replay.jpg

docs.title: Read-Only Device State
docs.text:
--device-state requests supported Tiny1C state information alongside capture. The legacy mailbox reader was implemented, not just a stub; native capture now uses the same field parser with Linux USBDEVFS_CONTROL, not libusb. Transfers are limited to 64 bytes and 50 ms each within the 250 ms mailbox budget. Cancellation, short replies, device replacement, permission failures and transfer errors produce explicit statuses without invalidating the saved image. Firmware fields may legitimately be unsupported, busy, invalid or unavailable; successful host tests do not establish readback on every firmware. Unavailable fields remain unavailable. It does not write firmware settings, prove physical gain or exposure accuracy, or provide a complete correction history. The image-only TDK mode does not support this Tiny1C readback.

On 2026-10-30, native USBFS readback was exercised on a PC-attached Tiny1C reporting firmware Tiny_V3.14_M. The first snapshot returned 16 fields, including gain selection, firmware, shutter, temperatures, emissivity and image-processing settings. Twenty further state-enabled captures all passed exact raw/embedded-temperature comparison while retaining five process file descriptors and four video mappings. This is PC evidence, not a MORA readback or endurance qualification.

The 250 ms budget does not guarantee all 20 fields in one snapshot. On this camera, later AGC fields and mirror/flip were timed out or skipped, and some following snapshots found the mailbox still busy. These statuses are retained; the driver does not extend the budget or pretend that missing readings were measured. Readback is after capture, not frame-atomic, and does not establish gain, shutter timing or correction settings at exposure. To change settings, use the separate explicit sensor controls; capture with --device-state never writes to the camera.

docs.title: Explicit Sensor Controls
docs.text:
Tiny1C hardware controls are standalone operations, not capture options. Stop any service or other process owning the camera first. Only one control is accepted per invocation; it cannot be combined with an output image, replay, capture-server, analysis, correction or rendering options. Nothing in normal capture or configuration-file loading automatically applies these writes.

Read and record original values before changing them:

bin/lwircam --get-control gain
bin/lwircam --get-control emissivity-128
bin/lwircam --get-control agc-mode
bin/lwircam --get-control agc

Select a particular camera with --device /dev/videoN or --serial SERIAL. The normal native device identity, exclusive ownership and USB permissions apply: the account needs read/write access to the Tiny1C USB node, which the supplied 99-tiny1c.rules grants to the plugdev group. These commands use Linux USBFS directly.

docs.title: What Each Control Does
docs.text:
Command Values What It Changes Use It When --get-control NAME gain, emissivity-128, agc-mode, agc Nothing; reads the current firmware value Recording settings before a change, or checking state after an uncertain result --set-gain low\|high low, high The sensor's physical measurement range. High gain gives finer temperature resolution over roughly everyday temperatures; low gain covers much hotter scenes at coarser resolution Scenes saturate (pixels pinned at the maximum) in high gain, or you need finer detail and the scene is not hot --set-emissivity-128 N 1-128 The emissivity the firmware assumes when converting radiation to temperature, in units of 1/128 (128 = 1.0, 122 ≈ 0.95, 64 = 0.5) Measuring a known surface type: most organic matter, water and painted or matte surfaces are about 0.95; bare polished metal is much lower --set-agc-mode N 0-5 The vendor's automatic contrast algorithm for the camera's own grey image plane Tuning the camera-supplied image appearance; it does not change the temperature plane --set-agc 0\|1 0 off, 1 on Whether that automatic image contrast is applied at all Wanting a stable, non-adapting camera image for comparison between frames --ffc none Triggers one flat-field correction (vendor OOC/B update); the internal shutter briefly closes to re-measure the sensor's offsets The image shows banding, fixed patterns or drift, typically after warm-up or a large ambient temperature change

Gain and emissivity affect the reported temperatures. The vendor defines AGC mode and AGC on/off as image-processing settings for the camera's own grey image; the temperature plane is not expected to change, but this has not been independently measured. LWIRcam's own rendering windows, palettes and percentile views are independent of both. --set-gain is the physical sensor setting, unlike --gain-label, which only names the gain recorded in metadata and correction-profile matching. During FFC the camera may briefly deliver shutter-closed or repeated frames; avoid triggering it while taking a capture you need.

docs.title: Output And Exit Status
docs.text:
On success the command exits with status 0 and prints one line:

LWIR_CONTROL_OK control=gain operation=read value=1
LWIR_CONTROL_OK control=emissivity-128 operation=write value=122 readback=122 verified=1
LWIR_CONTROL_OK control=ffc operation=trigger acknowledged=1 verified=0

For gain, value=1 means high and value=0 means low. A write succeeds only when the firmware reads back the requested value. FFC reports acknowledgement only: the camera completed the request, but correction quality is not measured.

On failure the command exits with status 1 and reports the control, a status (timeout, busy, io_error, invalid, unsupported or cancelled) and whether a command was submitted. submitted=0 means the camera was not changed. submitted=1 means it may have changed even though completion was not confirmed; read the value back before deciding what to do next. Invalid values or combinations exit with status 2 before the camera is touched.

Each operation first acquires a fresh valid stream frame, without repeating the initial-power-instance-only eight-frame qualification; the camera's control channel does not reliably answer before streaming frames. Property setters send one command and then require matching targeted readback. This confirms firmware readback, not physical temperature accuracy or exposure-time settings. Standalone targeted reads bypass the short all-fields snapshot budget.

Ordinary setters and targeted reads have a one-second mailbox budget; gain and FFC have five seconds. FFC includes a three-second correction interval, then checks mailbox completion. These intervals apply only to explicit controls, never the normal capture hot path. The usual process supervisor still bounds the complete invocation.

After any transfer error, timeout, cancellation or mismatched readback, inspect the reported submitted flag. Never automatically replay a write or FFC. Use --get-control to inspect current settings, then explicitly decide whether to restore a previously recorded value. FFC is not flash calibration programming; this API issues no save-to-flash, firmware-update or factory-reset commands. Do not assume firmware settings are persistent across power cycles.

Changing physical gain or emissivity affects measurement interpretation. Keep correction profiles and gain labels consistent and validate against independent references. These APIs do not attach exposure-qualified setting history to later photographs. No new flight-controller control protocol is introduced.

On 2026-10-30, PC-attached Tiny1C hardware tests changed and read back gain high/low, emissivity 128/64, AGC mode 0/1 and AGC enable 1/0, restoring each recorded original afterward. One FFC request was acknowledged. A following JPEG passed exact raw/embedded-temperature comparison with all 49,152 native temperature samples valid. Other firmware versions and MORA runtime remain separate validation requirements.

docs.title: Measured Correction Profile
docs.text:
Use --corrections only with a profile established for the matching camera, gain label, dimensions and temperature range. An operator-supplied gain label is not physical gain readback. Keep the original samples and validate any correction on independent references.

Start with the temperature-check procedure, not arbitrary example coefficients. Display palettes and lens calibration cannot replace temperature verification.

docs.title: Correction File Format
docs.text:
The flat INI uses these fields. Replace the identity/range and any fitted values with your camera's measured, independently checked configuration:

format=LWIR_CORRECTIONS_V1
serial=YOUR_CAMERA_SERIAL
gain=YOUR_GAIN_LABEL
width=256
height=192
scale_ppm=1000000
offset_mk=0
range_min_raw=18000
range_max_raw=22000
bad_pixel_count=0

This shows an identity scale/offset and example support range, not a measured correction. Raw units are kelvin times 64. The width/height, serial and gain label must match the input, and the support range must stay within the temperatures you verified. Unsupported readings are marked rather than extrapolated. List measured bad pixels only when you have established them; do not copy another camera's defect coordinates.

Apply a reviewed file with --corrections /absolute/path/corrections.ini and its matching --gain-label. Original samples remain available; display correction does not write firmware calibration tables. Save the file and independent checks together so the result can be reproduced.

docs.title: Use With USHER
docs.text:
For a reviewed live bench configuration:

./usher --lwircam --lwir-config /absolute/path/thermal.ini

A small capture policy might contain:

format=LWIR_CONFIG_V1
width=256
height=192
warmup_ms=5000
timeout_ms=20000
palette=iron
legend=1

Those dimensions are a Tiny1C example, not the TDK stream. Use the actual camera mode. Select a new directory/session for new observations and keep service changes separate from standalone camera checks.

docs.title: Geographic Hotspots
docs.text: Use the calibration workshop to measure lens geometry and mounting and check independent targets. Geographic analysis also needs usable observation pose/timing and the appropriate analysis build profile. A detected hot region is not automatically a fire or a surveyed location.

docs.title: Optional ONNX Classification
docs.text: Choose the assignment in lwircam_settings.ini, then use --check-model before --analyze on an existing image. Models requiring temperature values cannot use an image-only TDK frame. Classification is separate from numerical temperature measurement and calibrated hotspot projection. Choose compatible model inputs.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem Check No camera or access denied Power, USB cable, selected serial and device permissions Temperature option rejected Whether this mode supplies a supported temperature plane Unexpected measurement location Native coordinates versus rotated display Changing brightness Fixed window versus scene-dependent percentile rendering Coordinates unavailable Analysis feature, reviewed calibration and valid pose evidence Implausible temperature Independent references, emissivity, reflections, gain state and calibration

Before combining sensors on MORA, check repeated capture, storage, timing and total board resource use with the intended services running.

docs.title: MIMIC: Fly With A Simulated Camera
docs.text:
MIMIC turns cached aerial imagery into camera views for a simulated flight. The aircraft's position and attitude determine what appears in each photo. USHER saves the JPEG and its available flight information just as it would for a camera observation.

Prepare a simulated flight | Simulation terms | Photo maps

docs.title: From Tiles To A Photo
docs.text: The cache supplies pixels; NPS supplies pose. Banking or turning the aircraft changes the next camera view. Panning the GCS map does not move the camera. The renderer uses a flat ground model, not reconstructed buildings or terrain.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Use a working fixed-wing Paparazzi NPS aircraft. Start with the shared demo setup; no MORA or camera is required.

docs.title: 1. Prepare The Map Cache
docs.text:
In PprzGCS, display aerial imagery at zoom 18 over the example route and enough surrounding ground to cover the camera footprint. The default cache is ~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map, with the configured zoom-18 JPEG layout (--mock-map-cache DIR on USHER selects another existing cache):

find ~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map -path '*/18/*/*.jpeg' | head

Missing tiles stop capture. MIMIC does not download missing terrain or substitute blank/generated fields. Prepare the cache while online before expecting an offline flight to work.

docs.title: 2. Prepare Your Aircraft
docs.text:
From the Sensoraia root:

make -j32 usher soda pangea camera-lens
./kickstart.sh

./kickstart.sh installs the Sensoraia flight plans, demo airframes and unified control panel into your Paparazzi conf/ directory.

docs.title: A Complete Simulated Flight
docs.text:
Start Paparazzi Center (cd ~/paparazzi && ./paparazzi), select userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_conf.xml, aircraft Easystar_3_MIMIC (or your own aircraft using flight_plans/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_mimic_pangea_demo.xml), and target nps, then click Build. In the Session tab choose userconf/SENSORAIA/sensoraia_demo_control_panel.xml and Sensoraia MIMIC PANGEA NPS, then click Execute. It starts Simulator, Data Link, Server, PprzGCS and native USHER together.

Wait for valid GPS and live telemetry, then select Takeoff. The example collects images on suitable survey legs near its nominal 100 m altitude. Look for newly saved camera JPEGs and a PANGEA map, not merely GCS shot dots. Let the normal landing finish and stop the session programs afterwards.

A photo map is made from saved camera photographs, rather than joining the input tiles directly.

The companion prints the fresh map directory. Original photos use the normal USHER output location. Preserve both for comparison. The session can be repeated with the same configuration; a new map is created for each run.

docs.title: Try A Single Photograph
docs.text:
For an existing NPS setup where you manage the other programs yourself:

./usher --local --mock-map --debug

Do not start this alongside a Center session that already owns USHER. Select the AIcam capture mask and use the GCS photo control once the aircraft is in a suitable simulated pose. Wait for completion before retrying.

For optical blur, exposure and shutter experiments, use the optional lens emulator. It retains the clean MIMIC photograph. The LOOM NPS session passes --mock-lens resources/camera_lens_aicam.json on its USHER command line by default; edit that --mock-lens argument in the Session tab to use a custom profile or remove it to disable emulation. The selected derivative, not the clean source, reaches LOOM's reference archive and neural input.

docs.title: Camera Geometry And Limits
docs.text:
The camera is fixed to the simulated aircraft. Height, heading, bank and pitch affect its footprint. The clean renderer uses an aircraft-centred 3-by-3 tile neighbourhood; a view extending beyond it may be rejected.

The default field of view is illustrative. These visible map pixels are not thermal temperatures or a physical exposure. Check the module's model and input requirements before treating the pictures as representative evaluation data.

docs.title: When A Photo Is Missing
docs.text: Symptom Check Cache check fails Zoom, imagery layout and coverage around the entire route GCS dot but no JPEG USHER's completion/error message and output permissions Rejected view during a turn Bank, height and footprint size relative to available tiles No new map Saved-photo availability and PANGEA's diagnostics Endpoint already in use Stop the previous session rather than starting duplicate peers

docs.title: Choose And Run An AI Model
docs.text:
Sensoraia can run compatible ONNX models on the CPU, using the same native inference support across its sensor applications. You choose a separate model for each job: a vehicle detector, sound classifier and sampling planner do not interpret the same outputs.

AI terms explained | Spottercam | Diplacam

docs.title: Choose A Model
docs.text:
Start with a model exported for the application you want to use. Keep its graph, descriptor, labels and any deployment metadata together. The filename extension alone does not establish compatibility.

Application The Model's Job Spottercam Return image boxes, classes and scores LOOMcam Provide features or an explicitly declared return vector; a trained homing model is not included EARcam Classify the declared microphone sample window LWIRcam Classify declared display pixels or supported temperature samples Diplacam Predict one denoising step used by the native measurement planner

Each application reads its own settings file, such as modules/spotter_cam/spottercam_settings.ini. A typical ONNX assignment is:

inference_backend=onnx
model=models/assignment/model.onnx
model_descriptor=models/assignment/model.ini
onnx_threads=1
inference_timeout_ms=2000

Paths in these settings are relative to the INI file, not your terminal. Use --settings /absolute/path/settings.ini to select another assignment. Keep the supplied descriptor with the graph: it records the expected input preparation, tensor layout and graph identity.

Spottercam and LOOMcam can also use a compatible IMX500 .rpk with the physical AI Camera. inference_backend=auto selects ONNX for .onnx or IMX500 for .rpk on hardware; during PC simulation or saved-image CPU analysis, Spottercam automatically probes sibling vehicle_yolo11n_int8.onnx and vehicle_yolo11n_fp32.onnx exports in models/ when model points to models/nn_vehicles.rpk. CPU inference does not require the camera's neural processor.

docs.title: Check The Assignment Before Capture
docs.text:
From the Sensoraia root, for Spottercam:

make -j32 spottercam CAMERA_CAPTURE=0
bin/spottercam --check-model --settings /absolute/path/spottercam_settings.ini

CAMERA_CAPTURE=0 builds without physical camera support. It still runs real model inference. Omit that switch when you need live camera capture. The model check does not take a photograph or establish detection accuracy.

docs.title: Try A Saved Picture
docs.text:
Use an original image representative of the model's intended camera input:

bin/spottercam --analyze /absolute/path/photo.jpg \
  --settings /absolute/path/spottercam_settings.ini --sequence 1

Inspect the result beside the original and read any reported rejection. Ordinary analysis leaves the input unchanged and writes the application's result sidecar. The module guide explains its result fields and limitations.

Saved images, MIMIC views and supported live cameras can feed the same model processing. Their provenance remains different: a real neural result from a simulated image is still not a real-flight measurement.

docs.title: Understand Empty Results And Errors
docs.text:
Result What To Do Model accepted, no objects found Keep the empty result; do not invent targets Descriptor/hash mismatch Restore the graph and descriptor from the same export Unsupported tensor layout or preprocessing Obtain a compatible export; do not change labels merely to silence the check Runtime library unavailable Use the matching packaged runtime for this processor and release Inference timeout or failure Read the diagnostic and stop relying on fresh model results until resolved

Explicit PC demos can use labelled random observations under their documented fallback rules. That is a simulation choice, not normal production error handling. A present invalid model must not silently become a random detector.

docs.title: Put The Assignment On MORA
docs.text:
Build and package on the PC using the deployment workflow. The release needs matching runtime libraries, selected model files and their settings. Review the module's package selection before activation; a successful local image run does not measure MORA's shared memory use or sustained processing rate.

Evaluate the model on independent examples resembling its intended use. Scores are not automatically calibrated probabilities, and changing the camera, height, lighting or sound environment can change performance.

docs.title: PANGEA: Make Maps From Photographs
docs.text:
PANGEA combines supported saved photographs into a georeferenced photo map. Start with the included teaching images, then try photos from a MIMIC flight or a camera with the required pose and calibration information.

Mapping terms | MIMIC flight | GCS map tiles

The map is assembled from the six saved camera views.

docs.title: Try It Without A Flight
docs.text:
From the Sensoraia root, build PANGEA and copy the teaching images into your own example directory:

make -j32 pangea
mkdir -p "$HOME/Pictures/pangea-example/photos"
cp modules/pangea/docs/images/pangea-photo-*.jpg "$HOME/Pictures/pangea-example/photos/"
bin/pangea --input "$HOME/Pictures/pangea-example/photos" \
  --output "$HOME/Pictures/pangea-example/map-01"

Use a new output name for a separate experiment. Wait for the map-published message, then open map-01/latest/map.jpg. The originals are unchanged. No flight, physical camera or online map connection is needed for this example.

docs.title: Make A Map During A MIMIC Flight
docs.text:
The MIMIC Center session starts capture and mapping together and prints a new map directory. PANGEA uses saved camera views, not direct stitching of the source provider tiles.

For a setup where you manage the other simulation components yourself:

./usher --local --mock-map --pangea "$HOME/Pictures/pangea-flight-01" --debug

Do not run that command beside a session already owning USHER. A missing map does not necessarily mean capture failed; inspect the saved originals and the mapper's own diagnostic.

docs.title: Use Your Own Camera Photos
docs.text:
For original USHER JPEGs with a matching measured camera profile:

bin/pangea --input /absolute/path/photos --output /absolute/path/new-map \
  --camera-profile /absolute/path/camera.ini

Add --watch if the directory will receive more completed photos. Otherwise the command finishes its backlog and exits. One camera, resolution and calibration belong together in a map.

The profile declares delivered image dimensions, lens geometry and mounting. Use the supplied examples/pangea/aicam-2028.ini only as an illustrative starting format, not measured calibration. Generic GPS-only JPEGs may lack the attitude/height evidence required by this workflow.

docs.title: Prepare The Camera Profile
docs.text:
Copy examples/pangea/aicam-2028.ini to your own camera.ini. Its fields describe the delivered JPEG, not just the sensor's advertised size:

Field What To Supply filename_prefix Original camera filename prefix, normally a, c or l width, height Actual JPEG dimensions in this mode fx, fy Focal lengths in image pixels, not millimetres cx, cy Principal point in the delivered image mount_roll_deg, mount_pitch_deg, mount_yaw_deg Measured mounting relative to the aircraft

Keep schema=PANGEA_CAMERA_V1. The supplied numbers are a nominal example; substitute measured geometry and mounting for your setup. Changed crop, resolution or optics can need a different profile. Use original upright photos, not pre-undistorted, cropped or annotated review copies.

For a live supported camera launcher, choose the actual backend and profile:

./usher --aicam --pangea /absolute/path/new-map \
  --pangea-camera /absolute/path/camera.ini

This is real capture. Review sensor ownership and service selection first. The visual-return LOOM profile is not this launcher's real-photo mapping mode.

docs.title: Completed-Survey Workflow
docs.text:
Use a validated capture manifest or survey CSV with the supplied examples/pangea/survey.ini format. Set input and new output paths for your survey, then check it before running:

bin/pangea --check /absolute/path/map.ini
bin/pangea --run /absolute/path/map.ini
Choice Use It For SIMPLE A simpler reference-plane composite on a desktop GREAT Seam selection, blending and completed XYZ tile output runtime.profile=auto Let the application select the supported resource profile

The bounded profile supports GREAT XYZ output; SIMPLE and orthomap exports use a desktop profile. Do not force a desktop workload onto a small board. Choose the tile zoom explicitly; higher zoom does not create source detail.

docs.title: Incremental GREAT
docs.text:
This workflow publishes provisional XYZ revisions as completed photos arrive, then produces a final tile pyramid. It is distinct from the ordinary live photo-map watcher and can run independently of USHER.

Copy examples/pangea/great-aicam.ini to your own session.ini. Set:

  • input.photo_directory to the original USHER photo directory.
  • input.camera_profile to your matching camera profile.
  • Start/end latitude/longitude to the region the photos actually cover.
  • mosaic.reference_plane_amsl_m to ground height in the same vertical reference as the admitted camera altitude; do not mix MSL and ellipsoid heights.
  • output.directory to a new map session.

Keep runtime.profile=low_memory for this AI-camera directory workflow, including when trying it on a desktop. The completed-survey profile choices above are a different input path.

The example chooses pose_policy=recorded for ordinary request-pose metadata. Choose exposure only when native capture provides qualifying observation- time evidence. Exposure mode rejects missing evidence rather than silently using a request pose. Neither choice certifies accuracy.

docs.title: Follow Completed Photos
docs.text:
Start capture separately, then run mapping in another terminal:

bin/pangea --follow-great /absolute/path/session.ini

This directory mode accepts completed top-level AI-camera a*.jpg originals with suitable metadata, not LOOM references or arbitrary GPS-only exports. Do not edit published originals while mapping. PANGEA reports rejected files and resource delays; starting a watcher does not promise an immediate revision.

docs.title: Timing Controls
docs.text:
The incremental follower reads these settings from the session INI:

[live]
update_seconds=30
batch_photos=4
cpu_percent=20
pause_file=mapping.pause
final_file=capture.complete

After the initial revision, changed input becomes eligible for another render when either four photos have accumulated or 30 seconds have elapsed since the last successful render. These are scheduling thresholds, not completion deadlines: validation, preparation and rendering still need time to finish. cpu_percent limits average process CPU use relative to one core, not the percentage of the whole computer. Its accepted range is 1..100.

Marker paths are relative to the INI directory. Create the pause file to defer processing, then remove it to resume. Create the final file only after capture and photo publication have finished. Pause and low-memory waits remain cancellable; a final marker does not override a pause.

The ordinary --watch photo-map path instead checks for two seconds of stable file identity using a monotonic clock, then publishes changed maps on its ten-second export cadence. A future-dated photo does not postpone admission; an explicit --since cutoff still filters source timestamps.

docs.title: Finish Or Resume
docs.text:
Stop capture and let pending tagging/publication finish. Stop the follower with Ctrl+C, then finalize the unchanged session:

bin/pangea --finalize-great /absolute/path/session.ini

For an interrupted run, repeat --follow-great with unchanged inputs/settings. Stopping PANGEA does not stop USHER. A finalized session is closed; choose a new output directory for another flight. Directory input uses GREAT's update/follow/finalize commands, not the completed-manifest --run path.

docs.title: Create Map Tiles For A GCS
docs.text:
Ground control stations display slippy Web-Mercator (EPSG:3857) pyramids of 256 x 256 tiles addressed as {z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg, with x increasing eastward and y increasing southward.

The quick --input ... --output ... replay command above writes one stitched latest/map.jpg (plus latest/map.vrt for GIS tools), not a slippy tile tree. To generate GCS-ready {z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg tiles from a directory of area photos, use processing.mode=great with output.format=xyz. PANGEA projects each admitted photo onto a UTM working grid, selects graph-cut seams, blends overlapping views across four frequency bands, resamples into Web Mercator, and writes clean 256 x 256 JPEGs without EXIF or XMP overhead.

docs.title: Choose Tile Zoom Levels And Staging Output
docs.text:
One XYZ run builds up to three consecutive zoom levels (min_zoom within two levels below zoom), deriving each lower zoom from aligned 2 x 2 child tiles so seams never jump when zooming in the GCS:

Zoom Ground Pixel (Equator) Ground Pixel (~52°N) Typical GCS Use 17 ~1.19 m ~0.74 m Approach and circuit overview 18 ~0.60 m ~0.37 m Standard flight-plan view; also read by MIMIC 19 ~0.30 m ~0.18 m Maximum built-in zoom of standard GCS satellite layers 20 ~0.15 m ~0.09 m Near-native low-altitude detail with a custom local GCS layer

Pick zoom to match your camera's actual ground sample distance rather than oversampling beyond optical detail. Always set output.directory to a new staging directory first—never directly to a populated GCS cache—because PANGEA refuses to overwrite existing {z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg files.

docs.title: Example 1: Directory Of Just-Captured USHER Camera Photos
docs.text:
Suppose you have just flown over an area with USHER AIcam and copied the folder of saved a*.jpg originals to $HOME/Pictures/area-flight-01/photos, together with your matching camera.ini (Prepare The Camera Profile).

Create $HOME/Pictures/area-flight-01/gcs-camera-tiles.ini from examples/pangea/great-aicam.ini:

[input]
photo_directory=/home/you/Pictures/area-flight-01/photos
camera_profile=/home/you/Pictures/area-flight-01/camera.ini
pose_policy=recorded

[start]
lat=52.0052
lon=4.3574

[end]
lat=52.0034
lon=4.3616

[processing]
mode=great

[runtime]
profile=low_memory

[mosaic]
reference_plane_amsl_m=0.2

[tiles]
zoom=19
min_zoom=17

[output]
directory=/home/you/Pictures/area-flight-01/xyz-session
format=xyz

[live]
cpu_percent=100

Key settings for a folder of photos you already captured:

  • [start] and [end]: Opposite latitude/longitude corners bounding the area your photos cover.
  • mosaic.reference_plane_amsl_m: Ground height of the surveyed field in the same vertical reference as the flight controller's navigation altitude.
  • runtime.profile=low_memory: Required for the AI-camera photo_directory input path even on a desktop PC. Setting cpu_percent=100 under [live] removes the background 20%-of-one-core throttle when running post-flight on a workstation.

Because all photos are already in the directory, you do not need to run the --follow-great watcher. Run one of these single-pass commands from the Sensoraia root:

  • Irregular flight path or partial bounding-box coverage — publish every strictly observed, 100%-covered 256 x 256 tile and omit unphotographed corners cleanly without gap invention:
bin/pangea --update-great "$HOME/Pictures/area-flight-01/gcs-camera-tiles.ini"
  • Complete lawnmower box coverage — finalize the session with graph-cut seams, multiband blending and source-derived gap completion across the entire [start]..[end] rectangle:
bin/pangea --finalize-great "$HOME/Pictures/area-flight-01/gcs-camera-tiles.ini"

Both commands publish the slippy tile pyramid at:

$HOME/Pictures/area-flight-01/xyz-session/latest/xyz/{17,18,19}/{x}/{y}.jpeg

docs.title: Example 2: Completed Survey Directory With Manifest Or CSV
docs.text:
When your photo directory contains a completed capture manifest (*.capture.ini, which already supplies [start], [end] and source_csv) or a validated survey CSV (*.csv) beside the JPEGs, use the desktop-capable survey runner based on examples/pangea/survey.ini.

Create $HOME/Pictures/area-survey-01/gcs-survey-tiles.ini:

[input]
capture_manifest=/home/you/Pictures/area-survey-01/photos/photos_session.capture.ini

[processing]
mode=great

[runtime]
profile=auto

[tiles]
zoom=20
min_zoom=18

[output]
directory=/home/you/Pictures/area-survey-01/xyz-staging
format=xyz
jpeg_quality=95

If you use source_csv=/path/to/photos.csv instead of capture_manifest, add [start] and [end] corner coordinates; on a desktop PC (profile=auto or desktop), you can also add complete_only=1 under [tiles] so flight lines that miss the corners of your [start]..[end] box publish all complete tiles and record omitted edge tiles instead of stopping.

Validate the inputs and tile plan first, then render across your PC's CPU cores:

bin/pangea --check "$HOME/Pictures/area-survey-01/gcs-survey-tiles.ini"
bin/pangea --run "$HOME/Pictures/area-survey-01/gcs-survey-tiles.ini"

The tile folders (18/, 19/, 20/) are written directly inside xyz-staging/, and the coverage report (dataset.json and tiles.csv) is saved beside it under pangea_exports/xyz_<session>/.

docs.title: Place And Use The Tiles In Paparazzi GCS (PprzGCS)
docs.text:
PprzGCS (pprzgcs) stores its local map cache by default under ~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map (configured by map/tiles_path in ~/.config/paparazzi/pprzgcs/settings.ini, or in pprzgcs --configure under Map → Tiles path). Inside that directory, each map provider uses:

~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map/<DIR>/{z}/{x}/{y}<format>

PprzGCS always checks the local disk cache before making any HTTP request: any {z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg file present on disk is displayed immediately, is never overwritten from the Internet, and works completely offline (pprzgcs --maps_no_http).

Choose one of the two cache placements below depending on how you fly.

docs.title: Option A (Recommended): Dedicated Local Layer In PprzGCS
docs.text:
Placing your PANGEA pyramid in its own cache subdirectory (map/PANGEA/) is the cleanest setup:

  • Your existing GOOGLE satellite cache stays untouched.
  • You can toggle Pangea Survey on/off and adjust its opacity slider right over the satellite base map in PprzGCS's Layers panel.
  • Setting addr="" prevents HTTP requests for unmapped surrounding tiles.
  • Setting zoomMax="20" (or up to 22) lets PprzGCS display sharp zoom-20+ tiles directly, whereas the built-in Google layer clamps at zoomMax="19".
  1. Copy only the numeric {z}/ zoom folders into map/PANGEA/ (from xyz-staging/ for --run, or from xyz-session/latest/xyz/ for --update-great / --finalize-great):
mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map/PANGEA"
rsync -av "$HOME/Pictures/area-survey-01/xyz-staging/" \
  "$HOME/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map/PANGEA/"

(For Example 1's camera-directory session, replace the source path with "$HOME/Pictures/area-flight-01/xyz-session/latest/xyz/" — keep the trailing slash so 17/, 18/, 19/ land directly inside map/PANGEA/ without session metadata files.)

  1. Register the local layer in your user tile_sources.xml. PprzGCS loads ~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/tile_sources.xml ahead of its system defaults (you can also open both folders from PprzGCS via File → Open app directory and File → Open user directory). Copy the default tile_sources.xml into your user directory once if it is not there yet:
mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs"
cp -n /usr/share/pprzgcs/tile_sources.xml \
  "$HOME/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/tile_sources.xml"

Edit ~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/tile_sources.xml and add your Pangea Survey <source> at the top of <sources> (PprzGCS assigns higher initial Z-order to earlier entries, so placing it above Google draws your fresh survey tiles on top of the satellite background automatically):

<sources>
 <source
     name="Pangea Survey" dir="PANGEA"
     addr=""
     zoomMin="18" zoomMax="20"
     tileSize="256"
     format=".jpeg"
 />
 <!-- keep existing Google, OpenStreetMap, etc. entries below -->

Match zoomMin and zoomMax to the zoom levels you generated (for example 17 and 19, or 18 and 20). If you do not add a custom 200 x 100 PNG at ~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/pictures/map_thumbnails/Pangea Survey.png, PprzGCS uses its default layer thumbnail automatically.

  1. Start PprzGCS and enable the layer: launch pprzgcs (add --maps_no_http for strictly offline field operation), open the Layers panel, enable Pangea Survey alongside Google, and zoom in to your surveyed area.

docs.title: Option B: Drop-In Merge Into PprzGCS's GOOGLE Cache
docs.text:
PprzGCS's built-in Google layer uses dir="GOOGLE", zoomMin="0", zoomMax="19", tileSize="256", and format=".jpeg"—the exact tile geometry and .jpeg extension PANGEA writes. Merging zoom 17..19 tiles into map/GOOGLE/ requires zero XML configuration and also feeds zoom 18 directly into Sensoraia's MIMIC simulated camera (GOOGLE/18/{x}/{y}.jpeg).

  1. Generate your tiles with zoom=19 and min_zoom=17 into a staging folder (built-in Google does not request zoom 20+).
  2. Optionally back up ~/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map/GOOGLE if you want to preserve prior cached satellite imagery over the same coordinates, then merge the numeric zoom directories:
mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map/GOOGLE"
rsync -av "$HOME/Pictures/area-flight-01/xyz-session/latest/xyz/" \
  "$HOME/.local/share/paparazzi/pprzgcs/map/GOOGLE/"
  1. Restart pprzgcs if it was already open (PprzGCS keeps already-loaded tiles in memory for the current window session). Outside your photographed patch and at coarser zooms (0..16), PprzGCS seamlessly surrounds your updated survey area with the rest of your GOOGLE cache.

docs.title: Map Files
docs.text:
Open the printed latest/map.jpg for a quick view. Geographic companion files, coverage information and export reports describe how the map is placed and which input contributed. Use those records when importing into GIS tools.

For the ordinary live/replay workflow:

File Use It For latest/map.jpg Quick visual view of the current map latest/map-mask.pgm Distinguish photographed coverage from missing ground latest/map.vrt Open the georeferenced map with transparent gaps in QGIS/GDAL latest/map.jgw JPEG world-file positioning; it does not identify a CRS by itself latest/map.json Geometry, input counts and source/profile information done/*.json Find accepted/rejected source records and their reasons

Black in the JPEG can mean missing coverage or real black image content; use the coverage mask or VRT to distinguish them. Map pixel spacing is not a measurement of geographic accuracy.

XYZ tiles are addressed by zoom/X/Y, not three-dimensional coordinates. A visually complete export can contain source-derived gap filling; it is not proof every output pixel was independently photographed. Neither SIMPLE nor GREAT reconstructs building heights or all terrain relief.

A completed GREAT export is a tile pyramid with a dataset.json report; PANGEA does not currently package it as one GeoTIFF. The ordinary live/replay map workflow separately provides the latest/map.vrt GIS view described above. For an interrupted survey, keep inputs and settings unchanged and rerun the same command to reuse a matching checkpoint. Changed inputs or calibration need a new job. Do not edit originals midway through a resumed survey.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem Check Photos rejected Required pose/height information, image orientation and camera profile No published map yet Wait for export, not just an assembled-photo message Doubled roof edges or seams Pose timing, calibration, terrain relief and overlap Existing output refused Use a new directory or resume the matching unchanged job Resource limit reached Use the appropriate resource profile and inspect the diagnostic Working input changed during checksum Stop edits or copying into published inputs; resume only with the original unchanged files Cannot hash or publish a working file Check that storage is available and the input is a regular file, not a pipe or symlink New tiles do not appear in PprzGCS Confirm numeric {z}/{x}/{y}.jpeg folders sit directly under map/<DIR>/, check zoomMin..zoomMax, enable the layer, and restart pprzgcs

Reference-plane maps can misplace elevated objects. Attractive blending and fine pixel spacing do not demonstrate surveyed geographic accuracy.

docs.title: Use The Raspberry Pi AI Camera
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi AI Camera is a visible-light camera built around Sony's IMX500 sensor. Sensoraia can use it for ordinary photographs, compatible vehicle detection or experimental visual return. Choose one profile at a time.

AI Camera terms | Spottercam | LOOMcam

docs.title: Connect The Hardware
docs.text: Power off before connecting or removing the ribbon cable. Use the cable matching the board's connector; the Pi Zero family needs the smaller Zero-compatible connection. Seat the cable squarely and close the latch. Check your board's camera/display connector documentation rather than assuming similar-looking sockets have the same role.

docs.title: Prepare Raspberry Pi OS
docs.text:
The current reference setup uses 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS Trixie and its camera tools, drivers and matching resources. MORA is not limited to a Pi, but using this camera on another board depends on a compatible camera stack and requires that board's own integration and validation. On the reference Pi:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install imx500-all

Use the distribution's camera documentation if that package is unavailable. Review OS/kernel updates as board maintenance: compatibility needs checking with the actual installed camera stack, not a dated version copied from a guide.

docs.title: Check Camera Discovery
docs.text:
Stop USHER and any other camera client before a standalone check:

rpicam-hello --version
rpicam-hello --list-cameras

Look for the IMX500. With no local display, take a photo without preview:

rpicam-still --nopreview --timeout 2000 --output ai-camera-test.jpg

Open the JPEG on your PC and check that it is sharp, correctly exposed and oriented as expected. Use the actual reported camera index when multiple devices are present. A nonempty file alone does not prove image quality.

docs.title: Choose A Sensoraia Profile
docs.text:
Profile Use It For --aicam Ordinary photographs using the OS camera tool --aicam --native-photo Native photographs without a model or rpicam-still --spottercam Compatible vehicle detection and same-image results --spottercam --native-photo Native photographs with Spottercam detection disabled --loomcam Experimental visual-return observations and bounded target policy

All three use the same physical camera. Do not start two owners, and do not run a standalone camera application beside an active USHER capture profile. Installing camera packages alone does not select a model or enable detection.

An IMX500 model uses a compatible RPK. A CPU ONNX model is a separate choice; see choose a model. Renaming an unrelated model does not make its outputs meaningful to the application.

docs.title: Deploy And Select A Profile
docs.text:
The full MORA package installs all camera workers ready to run. You do not need to hand-edit systemd service templates to switch between them—simply set CAMERA in camera.conf at the Sensoraia root (or pass CAMERA=<name> on the make command line):

Desired IMX500 MORA Mode camera.conf / Command-Line Selection Resulting Service Command Plain AI Camera photos (native libcamera, no model) CAMERA=aicam usher --aicam --native-photo Spottercam (default: IMX500 + nn_vehicles.rpk) CAMERA=spottercam usher --spottercam LOOMcam (visual-return homing) CAMERA=loomcam usher --loomcam

(Advanced: if you specifically want OS rpicam-still instead of --native-photo, or --spottercam --native-photo, you can customize ExecStart in usher.service.in directly.)

From your PC checkout, build, upload, and activate the AI Camera profile in one step:

make mora-deploy CAMERA=aicam MORA_SSH_TARGET=air@theatre.local
ssh air@theatre.local 'systemctl --no-pager --full status usher.service'
ssh air@theatre.local 'journalctl -u usher.service -n 50 --no-pager'

Adjust the SSH target and MORA_INSTALL_DIR for your installation. Deployment rebuilds the ARM64 package on the PC, stages it on MORA, checks dependencies and restarts USHER. The packaged service uses its configured UART; send a camera-2 request from the connected flight controller and inspect the saved image under the service account's ~/Pictures/sensoraia/. Filenames begin with a, and existing photographs are not overwritten. See the complete deployment procedure for setup, password handling and recovery.

docs.title: Native Photographs
docs.text:
For photographs without object recognition, select either native photo mode:

./usher --aicam --native-photo
./usher --spottercam --native-photo

Both use the same libcamera capture and JPEG code. The AIcam selection starts bin/aicam; the Spottercam selection starts bin/spottercam without a model. Neither starts rpicam-still, loads a model or produces detection results. USHER also skips SODA analysis for these photo-only captures. The IMX500's previously retained network is cleared from volatile sensor state; its model file is unchanged and a later detection session loads it again.

Each request waits for a new frame and saves a 2028x1520 JPEG at quality 90 with 4:2:0 sampling and sensor timing evidence. The camera and storage determine the available rate. Use the camera speed test to measure your setup. A failed native capture is not replayed through another backend. --native-photo cannot be combined with mock capture or detector settings.

Option Purpose --aicam Select ordinary AI Camera photographs; without --native-photo, use rpicam-still --spottercam Select the same IMX500 for vehicle detection, or photo-only capture when combined with --native-photo --native-photo Use the native libcamera worker without a model, detector, SODA or rpicam-still --speedtest Take one warm-up and ten timed photographs, report the observed rate, then exit USHER_AI_CAM_TIMING=1 Log native acquisition and JPEG-save times; useful for diagnosing capture latency

If the native worker fails during a request, that request fails without an automatic replay. A later request can start a replacement worker after the old one has exited. Check the service journal and storage space if failures repeat.

For a standalone photograph, stop other camera owners and choose a new absolute output path:

./bin/aicam --probe
./bin/aicam --capture /home/air/Pictures/aicam-photo.jpg
./bin/spottercam --photo-only --probe
./bin/spottercam --photo-only --capture /home/air/Pictures/spotter-photo.jpg

Run these from /home/air/sensoraia on MORA, after stopping USHER if it owns the camera. --probe checks that a frame is available without saving a JPEG; --capture saves one new file and exits. Restore the service afterward. The target needs its compatible libcamera runtime, IMX500 driver and Raspberry Pi camera tuning files; no model is needed for native photo mode.

For a short throughput measurement, follow the camera speed test, selecting either ./usher --aicam --native-photo --speedtest or ./usher --spottercam --native-photo --speedtest. It stops and restores the service manually around the standalone measurement and retains the test photographs.

docs.title: Capture Through USHER
docs.text:
After the board/sensor check, select the intended backend in your reviewed service configuration and follow deployment. For a separately managed live bench session with no other owner:

./usher --aicam --debug

Connect the prepared FC/UART integration and request one photo. Check both the saved JPEG and its available flight metadata. Use the capture guide for service diagnostics and result interpretation.

docs.title: If Something Does Not Work
docs.text:
Check cable seating and power before software changes. A busy-camera error often means another application owns it. For model failures, inspect the module's descriptor/export requirements rather than switching randomly between RPK, ONNX and camera-tool configuration files.

Camera mode, crop, delivered dimensions and mounting affect geometry. A nominal product field of view is not a calibration of your installed camera.

docs.title: Prepare a Pi Zero 2 W for USHER
docs.text:
This guide covers the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W reference board and its current 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS Trixie setup. MORA means the onboard compute role, so a different suitable board may be used; its OS, UART, drivers, runtime packages and deployment need board-specific setup. These Pi instructions are not universal.

When this guide says OS image, it means the single operating-system file you flash onto a microSD card—not a camera JPEG—and flashing simply means writing that operating system onto the card so MORA can boot from it.

Use the official Raspberry Pi Imager to write Raspberry Pi OS to a microSD card. The steps below cover first access, the camera UART and network settings you may need away from the desk.

Before flashing, make sure the selected Wi-Fi network is reachable by a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It supports 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi; use WPA2-Personal or a WPA3-Personal network verified to work with the selected image and access point. Avoid enterprise authentication and legacy TKIP.

  1. In Imager, select Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS Trixie headless image, and the intended microSD card. Confirm its capacity and name before continuing: writing erases the selected card.
  2. Open OS customization. Set a hostname, a non-default user, the Wi-Fi network and country, then enable SSH. Prefer public-key authentication; paste the public key from the development PC into Authorized keys.
  3. Write the card and wait for Imager's verification to succeed. Eject it, insert it into MORA, and power the board.
  4. From the development PC, confirm the configured account and network work:
ssh air@theatre.local

This example uses the project's default account and hostname. Substitute the username and hostname you configured in Imager if they differ. The .local name requires mDNS support on the development PC and local network; if it does not resolve, use the board's DHCP address from the router instead.

For Imager-specific screens and recovery options, see the official Raspberry Pi getting-started documentation.

docs.title: Fast SD-Card Backup, Cloning, And Auto-Expanding Restore
docs.text:
Configuring Raspberry Pi OS, Wi-Fi, SSH keys, UART overlays, device groups, and camera tools from scratch takes real effort—and microSD cards at an airfield occasionally get lost, soaked, or corrupted right before flight day. Sensoraia ships two Linux PC helpers in build-support/ that turn your finished "golden" MORA card into a small archive you can clone onto spare cards in minutes:

  • Why this saves so much time: A plain whole-card dd reads every single empty gigabyte on a 32 GB, 64 GB, or 128 GB card. Instead, build-support/fast_sd_backup.sh inspects the partition table (sfdisk), reads only up to the last sector actually used by your partitions, shows a live progress bar and ETA (pv), and compresses across all CPU cores in parallel (xz -1 -T0). When restoring or cloning onto a new card, build-support/fast_sd_restore_and_expand.sh streams the image straight to hardware and automatically expands the EXT4 root partition to 100% of the destination card (parted + e2fsck + resize2fs) before you even eject it—no extra resize dance on MORA needed!

Install the standard Linux disk utilities once on your PC if needed (sudo apt install pv xz-utils parted e2fsprogs util-linux), shut MORA down cleanly, and insert its microSD card into your PC.

  1. Back up your configured MORA card (confirm the whole-disk device name such as /dev/sdX or /dev/mmcblk0 with lsblk—never a partition like /dev/sdX1):
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,TRAN,MOUNTPOINTS
sudo bash build-support/fast_sd_backup.sh /dev/sdX /path/to/mora-golden.img.xz
  1. Clone or restore onto another microSD card (at least as large as the used partition boundary; this erases the entire target card, so double- check lsblk so your laptop's own SSD stays safe and happy):
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,TRAN,MOUNTPOINTS
sudo bash build-support/fast_sd_restore_and_expand.sh \
  /path/to/mora-golden.img.xz /dev/sdY

Wait until the script prints ==> Restore and expansion complete! before removing the card. Keep two cloned cards in your flight box and future-you will thank present-you. (For flashing a brand-new blank OS for the very first time, Raspberry Pi Imager remains the easiest starting point.)

docs.title: Configure UART for USHER
docs.text:
On MORA, disable Bluetooth and dedicate the full UART to USHER. Run the following on MORA, then reboot:

sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt

Under the existing [all] section in config.txt, add:

enable_uart=1
dtoverlay=disable-bt

Save the file, then open raspi-config to turn off the Linux login prompt on that serial port (an autopilot and a Linux login prompt make terrible conversation partners):

sudo raspi-config

In raspi-config, select Interface Options > Serial Port, answer No to the login shell, and Yes to serial hardware, then reboot:

sudo reboot

After reboot, log back in and verify the UART device mapping and group membership:

ls -l /dev/serial0 /dev/ttyAMA0
id -nG

Expected mapping: /dev/serial0 -> ttyAMA0. The account running USHER must belong to dialout; if dialout is not listed yet, add it once:

sudo usermod -aG dialout air

Log out and back in so the new group membership takes effect.

docs.title: Preventing Sleep and Suspend States
docs.text:
Raspberry Pi OS normally does not suspend a headless Pi. If a board is managed by software that might request suspend, disable those targets explicitly:

sudo systemctl mask sleep.target suspend.target hibernate.target hybrid-sleep.target

If you do not like the change for whatever reason, to reverse the change later, run:

sudo systemctl unmask sleep.target suspend.target hibernate.target hybrid-sleep.target

docs.title: Save Multiple Wi-Fi Networks
docs.text:
Raspberry Pi OS Trixie uses NetworkManager. You can save more than one Wi-Fi profile so MORA can connect to a known network when it is available. Configure each profile for a network you expect MORA to use in the field.

Check the Wi-Fi interface name on MORA:

nmcli device status

It is usually wlan0. Add each network, replacing the example SSIDs and profile names. --ask prompts for a password instead of putting it in shell history or the process argument list:

sudo nmcli --ask device wifi connect "Desk SSID" ifname wlan0 name "Desk WiFi"
sudo nmcli --ask device wifi connect "Field SSID" ifname wlan0 name "Field WiFi"

NetworkManager saves each profile. To prefer one when it chooses among available autoconnect profiles, assign it a higher priority (the valid range is -999 to 999):

sudo nmcli connection modify "Desk WiFi" connection.autoconnect-priority 20
sudo nmcli connection modify "Field WiFi" connection.autoconnect-priority 10

A higher priority is considered first when NetworkManager selects a profile to autoconnect; it does not disconnect an already active network just to switch to a higher-priority one. Check saved and active profiles with:

nmcli connection show
nmcli connection show --active

For a network that does not broadcast its SSID, add hidden yes to the connect command and provide the SSID explicitly. Hiding an SSID is not a security measure and can cause clients to probe for that network:

sudo nmcli --ask device wifi connect "Hidden SSID" ifname wlan0 name "Hidden WiFi" hidden yes

docs.title: Add Wi-Fi Before First Boot
docs.text:
Use this recovery path when MORA has no network connection and you cannot reach it over SSH. It requires a Linux development PC with an nmcli version that supports --offline, plus a way to read the microSD card. The saved profile contains the Wi-Fi password, so keep the card secure.
